items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I seek leave to table a table showing the 85 percent increase
in the number of dairy cows nationally between 1990 and 2013. It is a table prepared for
the Green Party by the Parliamentary Library.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On the basis that it may not be freely available and may be useful
for the House, I will put the leave. Is there any objection to the tabling of that table?
Leave has been denied.
Small Businesses—Confidence and Accident Compensation Levies
12. JONO NAYLOR (National) to the Minister for Small Business : What reports
has he received about support for measures the Government has taken to assist small
business?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: According to the latest Mind
Your Own Business (MYOB) business monitor survey of over 1,000 small and medium
businesses, 65 percent trust this Government’s management of the economy, up from 63
percent just prior to the election. The Government’s handling of the economy and our
sensible policies have been identified as some of the reasons that New Zealand’s small
and medium businesses continue their approval of this Government. This Government
will continue our support for small and medium enterprises. We are committed to
delivering on our policies through the Business Growth Agenda, the Better for Business
programmes, and, of course, all those that help support small and medium enterprises to
grow more and employ more Kiwis.

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: What measures is the Government undertaking to help support small
and medium businesses?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: This Government is delivering on a number of measures to
support growth of small and medium businesses. These include making it easier to
employ staff by implementing the 90 -day trial, the starting -out wage, simplifying the
way small businesses interact with the Government via the New Zealand Business
Number, rolling out ultra-fast broadband, reducing personal and company tax rates, and
reducing compliance costs under the Better Public Services targets. These policies and
others show again that this Government is better for business.
2356 Oral Questions 18 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: What factors would stifle the growth of small and medium business?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: According to the MYOB report, small and medium businesses
want to focus on growth, innovation, and employment. The last thing small businesses
need is to have to spend more time, effort, resource, and money on things such as new
and complex taxes, unionised workplaces, and large minimum wage increases. Those
factors are, in fact, still proposed by the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Has he received any reports from small business representatives or
small businesses themselves supporting the Government’s decision not to further reduce
ACC levies by $350 million in line with ACC’s recommendation last year?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Just last night, actually, I was at a function for about 130- odd
small businesses in Hawke’s Bay. And a few of them —we did discuss, actually, the
$1.5 billion of ACC reductions that have already be en announced, banked, and locked
in by this Government. Those same organisations also talked about the need for
certainty, transparency, clarity, and a sustainable accident compensation system within
New Zealand, which would not happen if in fact the membe r were to get her political
hands on setting the levies of ACC.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can the Minister explain how ACC was incorrect in proposing to
the Government that it would be sustainable to reduce ACC levies by $350 million for
small and medium sized enterprises?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: If that member had been listening via various question times
over the last week, she would have seen, and probably heard, that the decisions that are
around the levy settings are actually a decisio n of Cabinet —such as the $1.5 billion
decision in ACC reductions that have already occurred.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I specifically asked the
Minister to explain—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume her seat. The question was asked, it
was a legitimate question, and on this occasion the answer addressed the question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is he saying that ACC was wrong to assert that levies could
sustainably be reduced for small and medium sized enterprises?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Well, part of that question you should address to the ACC
Minister, but, in fact, small and medium sized enterprises in New Zealand are enjoying
the benefits of the $1.5 billion per annum —now locked in—reductions of ACC, while
balancing the need to have a strong, sustainable ACC system that brings certainty to
small and medium enterprises in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Will he ask the Small Business Development Group, at its n ext
meeting, whether it supports ACC’s proposal that levies for small and medium sized
businesses be lowered immediately by $350 million?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: In my ongoing discussions with members of that group and, in
fact, with many, many others in the small business community, they all value the $1.5
billion reduction of ACC levies they are already enjoying and banking. Of course,
businesses always like lower costs, but at the same time they like transparency,
certainty, and sustainable agencies of Government such as we have with ACC now.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Small Business
Development Group is meeting in the Minister’s electorate very soon. I simply asked
whether he would put one question to it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree, and I am going to invite the member to ask that question
again.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Will he ask the Small Business Development Group, at its next
meeting, whether it supports ACC’s proposal that levie s for small and medium sized
businesses be lowered immediately by $350 million?
18 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2357

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I would very much prefer not to pull or drag that group into
some political sphere. It provides good policy advice and discussion, in fact, in and
around other issues, such as locking in the $1.5 billion reduction of ACC levies that
have already been locked in. But I welcome that member’s interest in the Small
Business Development Group, and she could read many of its reports. In fact, it would
be quite good if she came in and supported its position, for example, on the 90-day trial.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of miscellaneous business . There is a lot to look forward to in New Zealand
right now. We have got the Northland by -election, we have got National continuing to
deliver for families, and, of course, we have got the Cricket World Cup quarter-finals.
I am looking forward to welcoming my new colleague Mark Osborne into Parliament
when he turns up here on Tuesday, 31 March after a great win in Northland. But what a
lively place it must be in Northland right now for the Labour candidate, because the
Labour candidate has no backing from the Labour Party hierarchy. Andrew Little does
not even want her to win, and that must be a terrible place to be. And have you seen any
Labour Party MPs up there? No. Where has David Cunliffe been? He has been stuck up
the kauri tree in west Auckland. But in the end he decided he might be more use on the
ground, although his leader had a slightly different opinion. Where has Phil Goff been?
He has been off campaigning to be the mayor. They are not backing her at all.
Meanwhile, Winston is wandering around promising to take action —flying around in a
helicopter promising to take action on the closure of fictional health centres, which were
never even opened. So it is all pretty strange up there. It is getting pretty wild.
But what I can say is that National is delivering for families in Northland. There is no
question about that. If you look at the area I am responsible for—health—there has been
a huge increase in what has been going on up there. Last year 8,500 Northlanders got
elective surgery there. We have been really tackling the tough problems of rheumatic
fever—a 25 percent decrease in the rate there over the past year. The initiatives around
healthy homes, the health promotional activity, the free sore throat clinics, the drop- in
clinics, the throat swab bing—we are really focused on these tough problems in
Northland. I can also say —you heard my colleague Steven Joyce today talking about
this—that there were 7,500 new jobs in Northland last year, 600 of which are full time.
Northland’s economy grew by 5.1 percent last year —that is the highest rate in New
Zealand. So it is all go -ahead in Northland. Of course, we have also got the Pūhoi to
Wellsford road coming up; we have got the broadband initiatives, which are going to
extend fibre-optic cable to places l ike Kaikohe, Kaitāia, Kerikeri. There is a lot to look
forward to in that part of the country: Treaty settlements are going ahead up there, the
Twin Coast Cycle Trail —that is going to inject $20 million into that economy over the
next 5 years; 250 new jobs for Northlanders. There is a lot to vote for, positively, in that
part of the country.
Of course, there is the outlook, economically, in New Zealand—3.2 percent growth.
That is massive. Wages grew 15 percent over the past 5 years, and there were 80,000
new jobs in New Zealand over the past year. Inflation is at 0.8 percent, while weekly
average wages grew 2.5 percent over the past year. Unemployment is only 5.7
percent—much lower than in Australia. And, of course, we know that Kiwis are
flocking back here. Meanwhile, the balance of payments deficit —that has shrunk to 2.6
percent of GDP and is getting smaller all the time. We are going to hit surplus this
year—that is under control. We are heading to 20 percent of GDP by 2020. It is looking
good, but we are continuing to focus on families so that 300,000 houses are insulated
nationwide under this Government. There has been an increase in paid parental leave.
2358 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
We are providing breakfast in schools. In education, Hekia Parata is providing
leadership, basically, by bolstering the teaching profession. Early childhood education
investment has been doubled. Homestart programmes are getting young Kiwi families
into new homes. We have reduced ACC levies. So, in short, Kiwi families are much,
much better off. And, of course, there is the progress in welfare. [ Interruption] What
does that mean, Mr Speaker?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That means you have 1 minute to go.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Oh, rightio. I thought it was the finger —never
mind. We have had 48 percent fewer teen mums on benefits since 2009.
Mr Speaker, I know you will agree the Black Caps have started winning since the
change in portfolio. It has been quite remarkable. The Cricket World Cup has been great
for New Zealand. John Key and Brendon McCullum back themselves. They are on the
front foot. Andrew Little is like someone going out to face the West Indies without a
box on—hesitant, fearful, wandering around the crease. New Zealanders back winners.
They back John Key. They are backing National, and go the Black Caps on Saturday for
a great world cup quarter-final.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: The Prime Minister’s parting shot at the
end of my questions to him today was that the kids whom  he talked to when KidsCan
was giving out raincoats all told him that they all had a raincoat, and that, in just the last
hour, has shocked a large number of pe ople—the Prime Minister’s statement. Not
because the children might have two raincoats —one more than they might need—but
shock at the  Prime Minister’s complete ignorance of the stress and responsibility that
children who live in poverty and hardship cope w ith every day. We are talking about
one in six kids in hardship and one in four kids in poverty, from the latest statistics.
Kids who live in severe poverty know that the public perception of poverty is that
poverty is a crime of which they are guilty —that it is a disgrace , that it is a shame that
the family will bear , and that it should be hidden from view. Why would a child tell a
complete stranger the truth about their impoverished life? Any interaction that the child
may have seen between their parents and Work and Income teaches them that they are
to blame for their circumstance and that they deserve to be treated with disrespect. Any
interaction these children see between their parents and a charity or a food bank , or at a
supermarket counting out the coins, teaches those kids that poverty is embarrassing, that
it requires you to swallow your pride , and that, if you suffer it for long enough, to lose
your pride altogether. Any interaction their child may have seen between the family and
virtually any ag ency or any authority, let alone authority figure, teaches that child that
you do not tell the truth. You do not tell the truth because the truth will get you and your
family into trouble. The truth will cause you harm, shame, embarrassment, and ridicule.
That is what admitting to hardship and poverty gets you.
So no child is going to tell a stranger, let alone the Prime Minister —whom they see
on TV every day; the ultimate authority figure—what their life is really like. How could
they possibly expose themselves or their families to even more shame and ridicule? And
the kids are right—they bear this responsibility every day. And they are right because at
every turn —especially from this Prime Minister —the Prime Minister has refused to
engage with the evidence  of hardship and poverty. Even his comment this afternoon
shows that he is ignorant. His comment about funding KidsCan shows that, actually, he
is not funding KidsCan because he agrees that there is a need. That is what the Prime
Minister exposed in his answers today. He is funding KidsCan because he sees that
there is a political advantage in doing so. It is prime ministerial largesse. That is why
the breakfast clubs are being funded, not because he agrees that there is a need.
If he agreed that there was a need, he would make sure that he fixed it. He would
make sure that no kid in this country went to school hungry and that there was breakfast
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2359
in every school for every kid who needed it; that there was lunch in every school for
every kid who needed it. But he does not agree that the problem is serious, so he is just
putting in a band -aid response and using public money to justify what he is doing. He
does not agree. It is a politically expedient act for him. That is why the Prime Minister
and National are refusing to support my bill. He is refusing even to accept the evidence
that comes to him from independent agencies showing the extent of the problem. And
he then tries to claim, by talking to kids who are poor and who are not telling him the
whole story a bout their lives, that he is right. He has no idea of what these kids’ lives
are like, and they are absolutely right to keep it from him. How could they possibly trust
this man to treat their lives with the respect that they deserve when he treats poor kid s
not as a constituency and as the ultimate responsibility —the reason why he is sitting
here in that chair —but he treats those kids as if they are political opportunities so that
he can excuse himself and justify his miserable actions. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Well, there ends the
lesson. I am sick and tired of being lectured to in this House by that member, Metiria
Turei, who makes thin gs up, who has no facts to back up what she says, and who
accuses our Prime Minister of being mean. In fact, the country went to the polls last
year and gave National huge support —an enormous mandate —to keep on with the
reforms and to expand the reforms that it was in the process of making to all New
Zealand families. The reality of that is that New Zealanders understand that this is a
Prime Minister who cares about New Zealand families. This is a Government that has
done a great deal for New Zealand famili es, not the least bit making sure that there is a
strong, growing economy that is providing more jobs for people, and we are seeing
more people in work now than we have ever seen before.
But let us talk about this issue of food in schools, and let us look at the accusations
that this Government led by John Key is mean. The reality is that now, currently, this
Government is funding fruit in schools. We expanded the programme that the Labour
Government put in, where half of it was being spent on administrati on. We have
expanded it so that there is fruit going into every single school —and vegetables, I have
to say—throughout the country. Fonterra is providing milk to schools, and fridges to put
the milk in, so that there is fruit and milk in schools. This Government is working with a
programme called KickStart Breakfast, which is working with Sanitarium and Fonterra.
Just last month we delivered the 3,400,000 th breakfast. Every school in the country is
able to take part in that, and the Prime Minister is absolu tely right —just under 800
schools are taking part in providing that breakfast. That is being funded by this
Government along with other companies.
KidsCan is also providing food support to schools. And it is really interesting that in
the talk that KidsCan  had with me, it said that it is providing lunches to about 300- odd
schools but that it does so in a discreet manner. It does not want those children to be
stigmatised. It just makes sure that the schools can deliver the programme. So up comes
a politician who is making a political point with photos and media, and there we are —
we have those children stigmatised, which is totally against the respect that KidsCan
was showing those children. KidsCan has also been funding raincoats, and the
Government has funded that initiative with half a million dollars. And it is also funding
nits. We put $900,000 into treating nits because that was recognised as a problem.
I just want to share with the House, when we are considering, as part of this
Government’s programme, reform of the Resource Management Act. This Government
put $900,000 into relieving children of nits. Part of that funding went to providing
specifically designed handbasins to wash the children’s hair in at school. It was a
fantastic idea and schools were d elighted. Let me tell you that in the 17 Hawke’s Bay
schools it took 6 months to get a resource consent through to install those handbasins —
2360 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
6 months. In Hawke’s Bay, 17 schools waited while that resource management consent
went through their local councils. That is ridiculous.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: What councils?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Hastings and Napier. The members that represent those
areas should be banging on those councils’ doors —6 months to get resource consents to
put handbasins in so that KidsCan could roll out the nit programme. Since it has done
that, of course, we have seen a huge response to that, and it has made a huge difference
to the lives of those children. They have discovered all sorts of skin diseases as a result
of it, there are nurses working with them, and it is a very good programme.
So the point is that this Government is providing enormous help to those families,
and for that member to stand up in this House and accuse our Prime Minister of being
mean and of supporting kids for only a political purpose is, I think, outrageous, because
he has shown enormous leadership on this and has made sure that the Government is
stepping in to help hundreds and thousands of New Zealand children throughout
schools.
None of tha t takes away from the responsibility of parents. We know that, because
the economy is growing the average wage is growing. The Minister of Finance said that
in the House today. The average wage is growing faster than inflation, so families
should be taking  care of children —that is their first responsibility —but where they
cannot, this Government is stepping in to help.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Before I begin my contribution I just want to point
out t hat the Prime Minister today, in this House, stood up and claimed that he had
personally asked children about their access to things like raincoats and lunches, and
that he then had the Minister of Education call schools individually to ascertain the
availability of lunches for students in the schools. Then we have the Minister who just
resumed her seat, Anne Tolley, pointing out that the most important thing we have to do
for children living in poverty is to make sure that we do not stigmatise them. If tha t is
the case, what is the Prime Minister doing standing up and individually questioning
children on whether or not they can get school lunches or have a raincoat to wear to
school?
If we were serious about not stigmatising children, the Prime Minister wo uld not
base his and his Government’s policies on anecdote and on his personal surveying of
children and their families. Yes, talk to principals; yes, ask principals what is going on,
but we already have every report we need. Multiple reports have been con ducted into
this issue. If that Government is serious about addressing issues, then surely the reports
that say that 17 percent of children are living in material deprivation —a figure that that
Government uses itself—would be the basis on which we design our policies. Listen to
the evidence. That is all that we are asking.
You know that things start getting a little bit rough in a Government’s third term, and
we have got multiple examples of that, not least the fact Craig Foss is managing to get a
patsy question in almost every question time. If that does not demonstrate that things are
little bit off then I do not know what does. But it is not just the Opposition that
experiences the torrid nature of a third- term Government; it is the public that does as
well, and no more so than the people of Northland. The Northland by -election
demonstrates how badly this Government is willing to put politics before people. It is an
extreme example of a Government that is not listening to the real needs of the people on
the ground, but is simply trying to dangle electoral bribes. They are not even
particularly good electoral bribes at that. We have had $70 million worth of bridge
double-laning proposed as part of this by-election—some of the lowest-priority building
projects. And that Government would know that, if it had talked to the people on the
ground. If it had talked to the people on the ground, it would know that road sealing,
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2361
filling in potholes, and even funding for the polytech are higher priorities for the peopl e
of Northland than double-laning bridges that the candidate cannot even name, except for
the one that he can see from his back door. If that does not demonstrate that it is politics
before people, even politics before the people that National is campaigni ng amongst,
then I do not know what is.

items.speaker: Hon Maggie Barry
items.text: Like Labour’s campaign in the north—non-existent.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: If the Government wanted to do something meaningful, Ms
Barry, it would provide jobs. If you wanted to do something meaningful you would
provide jobs for the people of Northland. The Government would make sure that wages
were being lifted for the people of Northland. It would make sure that the schools in
Northland had everything they needed to provi de adequately for the children of
Northland. Seventy million dollars could go quite a long way in making a difference for
those people.
If we want another example of politics before people I would use the numbers that
were displayed in the New Zealand Her ald today around access to justice. Judith
Collins in 2012 decided that she was going to crack down on legal aid.

items.speaker: Hon Maggie Barry
items.text: Support Labour’s candidate.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Listen up, Ms Barry, you might actually learn something
meaningful. In 2012 Judith Collins decided that she would send out 47,000 letters on
outstanding debt—47,000 letters. A quarter claimed that they had an inability to repay
that debt—11,000 people went back to the Ministry of Justice and sai d they could not
pay. The Ministry of Justice substantiated those claims in how many of those 11,000
cases? In 10,000 of them. If that is not a red flag that that Government needs to look at
legal aid thresholds, then I do not know what is. If you will not  listen to us, listen to
Frances Joychild, listen to Justice Winkelmann. They have all raised red flags over what
is happening to access to justice in this country. This Government needs to make sure
that it puts people before politics, or is it that the justice system needs a by -election to
get a little attention?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak in this
debate. The first thing I want to do is address a couple of issues that were raised by the
previous speaker, Ms Ardern. To get a lecture from the Labour Party about what the
people are saying in Northland is ridiculous. There have been no Labour MPs there for
a very long time because they are no t campaigning there. They have left Willow -Jean
Prime under a bus, and we know that. I was doorknocking there at the weekend, and I
can tell you what they have been saying. Many people do believe that National has done
more than any other Government, but the reality is that the people of Northland do need
more, and the reality is that they do understand that there are more free doctors visits for
under-13-year-olds and more money to fix their schools. There are a number of schools
that have been fixed up in Northland. We have made more of an investment than ever
before in terms of those schools. There is more money in early childhood centres. There
is more money to insulate houses.
So a huge amount has been done, but the reality is that it is actually at ti mes like this,
when we see the situation with Cyclone Pam, that we see the best of New Zealand. I
have seen the best of New Zealand over this period. It is the case that it was
communities like Northland that won the civil defence award this year. They won that
award because despite massive challenges in terms of weather, we saw communities
rally together and help others. We have seen that in spades across New Zealand over
this period.
If I have learnt three things as the Minister of Civil Defence it is th is. The first is that
our hearts go out to the people of Vanuatu for everything they are dealing with. Some of
the unsung heroes in New Zealand in terms of civil defence are our engineers. What we
2362 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
do know in this country is that sometimes the difference between having massive loss of
life and people being saved is the buildings. We have seen that in Vanuatu. One of the
most powerful moments I have had as a member of Parliament was sitting with the
Minister from Haiti and talking about an event similar to Ch ristchurch’s earthquakes.
We lost several hundred people; they lost more than 250,000. That is the difference, so I
want to pay tribute to the engineers of this country.
The second thing is I want to say is what an amazing job so many regions across
New Zealand did to prepare for this event. We had evacuations in parts of Gisborne. We
had so many community groups on the ground doing amazing things. In the Chatham
Islands they still have a local state of emergency. I want to acknowledge the mayor and
the civil defence staff for what they are doing over there. They are still getting a bit of a
battering, but we will be there to help them.
So my message is that this is a Government that cares. We have demonstrated in
many communities —whether it is through und er-13-year-olds going to the doctor for
free, or whether it is through our investment in early childhood education or fixing more
schools than ever before —that we do care. But often we see the best of communities
right across New Zealand at a time like a civil defence emergency, when the only reason
that we get through these events is that communities rally, not just the people in
Wellington who are doing things from a civil defence perspective.
We have seen the best of New Zealand, and that is why I am very proud to be the
Minister of Civil Defence and to be seeing so many people on the ground helping others
at a time like this. Part of that is due to some of the changes we have put in place, like
shifting the Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management into the Department
of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, so that agencies across New Zealand rally at a time
like this.
So I want to acknowledge the people of Northland for winning that civil defence
award this year. I want to acknowledge the many fami lies I have met through my
doorknocking and the fact that they have acknowledged what this Government has
done. But I also acknowledge that there is more to do there in terms of investing in
education and infrastructure, and , with a National MP, we are the only Government that
can provide that.
I also want to acknowledge all of the people across New Zealand who have helped
others through this period, including the people of the Chathams, who are going through
quite a bit at this point in time.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I must admit I found it quite amusing when
the last speaker, Ms Kaye, talked about Northland and how Labour was disconnected,
and then she realised that over three -quarters of the  people sitting on this side of the
House have actually been up there and spoken to the people of Northland. One of the
most enlightening things for me is that I made a few visits and then I went to a local
pub. I started talking to the people about who they are going to vote for, and they said to
me: “We used to vote National, but we are sick to death of being taken for granted by
this Government.” They said they were going to vote for Winston Peters. I said:
“Really? You’re really going to vote for Winston? Why are you going to do that?”, and
they said: “National has taken us for granted for so long, and we’re sick to death of it.
We’re absolutely sick to death of it.” The thing is that we all know that by -elections are
often referendums on a Government’s performance. Well, I think that this will be a very
strong referendum on this Government’s performance, and I think this Government is
going to get a very big shock.
The other thing I found quite amusing is that the Hon Anne Tolley stood up and said
she is sick and tired of being in this House. Well, I have some very good news for the
honourable Minister. I was up in Whakatāne and Ōhope recently, and we had three
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2363
fantastic people who want to be the Labour candidate for the East Coast electorate. So,
Ms Tolley, do not worry about it. You will not be there in 2017.
Once again, that electorate will be returning to Labour, and I can tell you why. The
reason is that wherever I go around provincial New Zealand people say to me: “We’ve
been forgotten by this Nati onal Government.” They say that if you own a house in
Auckland or if you are involved in the rebuild in Christchurch, you are probably doing
OK. Even the guy who was the chair of Local Government New Zealand, the Mayor of
Hastings, who used to be a support er of this National Government, came out and said
that this Government does not have a strategy for the provinces. This Government has
no plan for the regions. I think that this is what we will be seeing in Northland. There
will be a very loud and clear message.
But the interesting thing is that I am back in my second term. I took a bit of break—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: A sabbatical.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I took a sabbatical. I took time out to talk to the people, to
reconnect with the people of the Napier electorate. But when I was in my first term, the
Government was quite an engaged Government. There was the Hon Simon Power who I
reckon, put through about 40 percent of the legislation on the Order Paper. He was a
very engaged and very hard -working Minister. There was John Key, who went out and
promised the world, and there was a National Government that was really driving what
it thought was an agenda. As we have since learnt, it was not a particularly favourable
agenda for the rest of New Zealand. But  when I came back to Parliament after 3 years,
goodness me, the change was immeasurable. It is like a lot of things. I think that if you
have been sitting here for the last 6 years, it is sort of incremental and you will not have
seen it. But coming back after 3 years, goodness me, the change is immeasurable.
There are a couple of things. Mr Joyce’s performance must be a worry to the Prime
Minister in terms of the way Mr Joyce has tried to arrogantly handle the Skycity
debacle, Northland, and corporate wel fare. The man is so out of touch with the way the
vast majority of New Zealanders think, it must be of concern to the Prime Minister.
There is no doubt about that. Then I was astounded, Mr Speaker —and you would
appreciate this—to hear the Deputy Prime Mini ster, the Minister of Finance, stand up
and basically say that you cannot trust anything a politician says during election time. I
thought that was despicable. I know that members on this side of the House go out there
and work really hard. We have key mes sages. David Parker spent an inordinate amount
of time costing a fantastic fiscal policy that was going to put the Labour Government
and New Zealand back on track. And then Mr English has the nerve to stand up and say:
“Don’t trust a politician during election time.”
Well, there is one thing I would like to say to the people of New Zealand: trust the
Labour Party. Trust everything we say, everything we will do and when we say that we
will stand for the people in regional New Zealand, when we say that we wi ll champion
those who have been forgotten by this Government, believe us because it is what we do.
We are a party that stands by what we say. We are not a party of empty slogans or
bribery, of throwing lollies out in a by -election. The Northland by -election is a
referendum on the performance of this Government and I think there will be a very,
very clear message sent from provisional New Zealand to that Government that it is out
of touch. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Whether or not the by-election
in Northland is a referendum on the Government’s performance, it will certainly not be
an endorsement of Labour’s, because its members cannot even support the ir own
candidate, let alone ask the people of Northland to support their candidate.
I want to talk about how this Government is supporting families and how we are
doing that through an integrated, client -focused investment approach with regard to
2364 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
families and vulnerable New Zealanders. This is a way of thinking that has been led by
this Government. It has been implemented over the last 6 years, and there is a lot more
work to do. It is something about which the former Labour Government had nothing to
say. When we came in, we set new targets. We are working towards those targets, and
we have seen results.
The net present cost of total benefits for the population of this country is $76 billion .
There are two key groups I want to focus on today. The first is teen sole parents. We
know that there are 2,600 teen sole parents, and, as Minister Tolley outlined today, that
figure has dropped by 50 percent since 2009 under this Government. We know that it
will be a 20-year average that those people will spend on a benefit, at a cost of $250,000
each, if they do not have a qualification. There are a number of steps that are being
taken by this Government to address that. One, we are putting a responsible adult with
each and every one of these people to provide them wi th budgetary support, to get them
back into education, and to get them a qualification, which will enable them to get back
into the workforce. We know that a teen solo parent who is under the age of 20 with no
qualification will spend an average of 20 year s on a benefit. If they can get a post -
school qualification, that average reduces from 20 years on a benefit  down to 7 years.
That is a considerable contribution towards these people’s lives and to the taxpayer.
There is another group of children I want to talk about, and these are children in care.
These are hugely disproportionate cost drivers for the Government. We know that there
are 2,000 males currently in care. B ased on 30 years’ worth of records from Treasury,
the Ministry of Education, the Ministr y of Social Development, the Ministry of Justice,
and the Department of Corrections all working together, we know that these kids are
destined for a life of involvement in the justice sector and correctional facilities if they
do not get back on track. The se are kids who are currently misbehaving in school and
going through foster home after foster home. There is one 10 -year-old foster kid in my
electorate who has been through 93 foster homes , and that is just unacceptable. I could
not imagine putting myself in the position of that kid mentally when he is getting
chucked from family to family , day on day, week on week, and then having to go to
school and try to get a qualification.
This Government has taken considerable steps to try to get these kids back on track
so they can have the life they deserve and the life  their coming families will deserve.
And what are we doing about that? We are implementing an individualised policy
approach led by Minister Tolley , formerly Minister Bennett, and Minister English. Just
going back to these 2,000 kids, we know that during their lifetime —if they do not get
back on track now —combined, they will have a collective cost to the taxpayer of $750
million in corrections system costs alone. So what do we do about that to try to get them
back on track, to try to improve their life chances? We are individualising the policy
around them, getting the Government departments to think of them as individuals and as
people instead of thinking about how departments best operate and work. That is what
we are doing.
Unlike Labour, our Government cares about individuals , and we care about families.
I can tell you how many young people receive sole parent benefits in my electorate. In
Gore there are 185, in Clutha District there are 168, and in Queenstown there are 98. In
Ōwaka, of the 228 people, nine of them are unemployed, three of them are on a sickness
benefit, six are on the domestic purposes benefit, and nine are on the invalid’s benefit.
We know individual people and where they are. We know their names, and Government
departments are now working with them to get them back into a better position.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: How many in Northland?

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Talking about Northland, we know who our candidate is, and
we fully get behind him and back him —Mark Osborne. Coming back, though, the most
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2365
compelling statistic I found was regarding the number of people who are currently in
correctional facilities. We have reduced youth crime and we have reduced recidivism
under this Government and under the integrated approach we are taking.
In conclusion, I want to fully support the steps this Government is taking under the
leadership of some very strong Ministers, who put families first, who put individuals at
the centre. We are improving public services, we are raising achievement standards, we
are reducing crime and recidivism, and we are improving the lives of families and
individual New Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Well, the one thing I can say for that young man Todd
Barclay is that he has got plenty of time on his side. He is a young man in the House, he
has got a lot to learn along the way, and there will be a day when he will realise that he
has not exactly been told everything by his associates that is actually truthful—is it?
There have been some speeches here this afternoon and I want to refer to a couple of
them. “The country gave this Government a mandate to carry on with its reforms.”
Really? Really —seriously? Well, I think the country gave New Zealand First a
mandate, by almost doubling the number of MPs that it has in this House, to curb this
Government’s excesses, to keep a choker collar around its neck, and to keep it honest.
That is the fact of the matter. There is almost double the number of New Zealand First
MPs in the House to keep this Government honest.
On 28 March rural, provincial Northland is going to send a message on behalf of
rural provincial New Zealand telling this Government that it is out of line, that it is out
of order. That message is coming and we are looking forward to the delivery of that
message.
One of the messages that Northland wants to pass back to this Government is that the
people there reject this Government’s amalgamation agendas. Oh, listen up—so too
does the Hawke’s Bay, and so too does the Wairarapa. If people are not listening now,
they damned well will be after 28 March, let us be sure about that. Let us have a look at
what the people are saying out there in rur al, provincial New Zealand. On the proposal
to amalgamate Northland, right, there were 1,800 submissions, of which over two-thirds
were opposed. In Hawke’s Bay, 732 submissions —heartland rural, provincial New
Zealand; listen up, listen up, team—said that 80 percent of them were opposed. Coming
to the greater Wairarapa, or the greater Wellington region—a Freudian slip; it should be
the Wairarapa region, should it not —there were 9,400 submissions. Those 9,400
submissions were overwhelmingly opposed to your Local Government Commission
lackeys’ proposal.
And what are they all so angry about? Listen up, National —what are they all so
angry about? They are angry with you, the National Government. Do you know why?
They are angry because you changed the Local Govern ment Act and you removed the
automatic right to a referendum. The National Government that is pushing these
reforms—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: They re-elected the Government twice after that.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: It has got a mandate for these reforms, b ut card-carrying members of
the National Party are overwhelmingly angry with you because you have taken away the
automatic right to a referendum. Do not talk to me about fighting for democracy. This
Government is anti-democracy. What else are those people angry about? They are angry
that when the Government forces a referendum by petition—

items.speaker: Hon Maggie Barry
items.text: They’re happy you’re gone.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: —listen up, Maggie, listen up—when you force a—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: —they force a referendum by petition, the referendum is right across
the whole Wellington region—
2366 General Debate 18 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Maggie Barry. I am sorry about that—Maggie Barry.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. He did correct it, but the
member well knows, as it is pointed out in the House, you must address a member by
their full name.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree. It is a robust debate, and I would be grateful, while the
member also gathers his breath, if he would stop drawing me into this particular debate.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It is the Hon Maggie Barry, and I want her to
listen up because those people are overwhelmingly angry that when the referendum is
conducted, it will be 400,000 people telling 40,000 in the Wairarapa what is best for
them. Talk to me now about sending troops to fight for democracy. That is anti -
democracy, and that is a hallmark of one of this Government’s reforms.
And who is out there right now, doing submissions, submitting towards the Local
Government Commission? Well, the Local Government Commission is hearing
submissions in the Wairarapa, and guess what sort of behaviour we are witnessing? We
are witnessing staff members from the Local Government Commission going over and
chatting, colluding, and giving advice to proponents of the super -city, and dismissing
and being arrogant towards card-carrying members of the National Party who oppose it.
Bring it on, we say in New Zealand First. Bring on 28 March, because there is a
shock coming. There is a shock coming, and the result will be a very, very emphatic
message to National from rural, provincial New Zealand. It  is tired of being taken for
granted. You have had 70 years to build 10 bridges —70 years—and you are promising
you are going to do them all next year. Well, hallelujah! Nobody is listening. Nobody
believes you. Power to the force for the north. Roll on 28 March. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Just looking at the opposite side, I wonder
who is the Opposition here —the Greens, New Zealand First, or the Labour Party. But
when I closely analyse this I see more ex -leaders sitting on the backbenches in the
Labour Party. So that must be the Opposition party then. But, unfortunately, its current
leader is also no better than their previously failed leaders, and that is because he  is not
backing his own candidate in Northland. When this Opposition Labour Party was in
Government for 9 years it created loads of inefficiencies. I say this because I still
remember how I felt in 2008 with this huge global financial crisis coming our way .
Then I am sure every New Zealander feared how they and their families and children
would get through this global financial crisis. What our new Prime Minister, the Rt Hon
John Key, then inherited from that Labour Government was this economy that was
already in recession, with Treasury predictions of doom and gloom and endless debt,
and this huge responsibility of navigating us through this global financial crisis.
I do not want to remember those nanny State days, when those members wanted to
tell our families what kind of shower fittings and lightbulbs we should be using. They
stood for more Government, more dependency, more rules, and more spending. But the
Rt Hon John Key and his Ministers, in 2008, focused the machinery of government to
deliver more for less. They did not increase taxes. They gave tax cuts across the board,
helping low and middle income New Zealand families. They did what they promised to
do, and that is what I call leadership. That leadership is working. The National
Government underst ands issues around our children and issues around our families.
National understands the worries of our senior citizens. It is not just about them being
safe and secure physically; it is about them being safe and secure financially and
socially too. New Ze aland families do understand the importance of our economy if
families are to flourish. National continues to stand with the families, and that is why
we keep investing in the public sector and we keep having challenging targets.
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2367
Just for an example, from 1 April next month paid parental leave is going to increase
from 14 weeks to 16 weeks. That is the National Government increasing it from 14
weeks to 16 weeks. From next year, on 1 April 2016, it will be increased by another 2
weeks, to 18 weeks. This ass istance will be extended to other families too. The parental
tax credit is going to be increased from $150 to $220 a week, and the length of that is
also going to be increased, from 8 weeks to 10 weeks. This is being done by the
National Government. This i s going to start from 1 April. After that, if we look at 1
July, free GP visits are going to be extended to children under the age of 13. Currently,
children under the age of 6 can access free GP visits and prescriptions, but the National
Government is investing to extend free GP visits to children under the age of 13. This is
an important precautionary health measure. It is expected that 400,000 primary school -
aged children will benefit from this investment, which is being done by the National
Government. This kind of assistance is really going to help our families and children,
because then families do not have to end up in the hospital queue at odd times. Because
of that, sometimes children miss their schooling and their suffering is longer as well.
All of this is complemented by keeping our houses warmer, drier, and healthier.
Around 300,000 homes are insulated, under the National Government, thanks to the

items.speaker: Warm Up New Zealand
items.text: Healthy Homes and the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart
programmes. Again, with our focus on children and families, the National Government
has partnered with Fonterra and Sanitarium to give free breakfasts in schools. This is in
all primary and secondary schools, regardless of their decile. This is to look after
children’s well-being, so that they do not suffer in their education if they are not fed at
home. Education is really important. National believes in delivering for all children.
National believes that we should provide opportunities to all our children to succeed.
That is w hy we are investing $359 million in communities of schools. This is to keep
our best teachers in classrooms to extend that leadership across different schools. Since
National came into office, the Government’s investment in early childhood education
has doubled. Our target is that 98 percent of young children are able to access some
kind of early childhood education programme before they start school.
The National -led Government, under the leadership of the Rt Hon John Key, will
continue to support our fam ilies and children. We will remain focused on the economy,
we will remain focused on jobs, and we will keep taking people off welfare because
employment is important. Employment is not just about money; it is much more than
that. We will continue to do that. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman): Last week I was
asked to resign—not by the National Party; no, indeed, it was by a community leader on
the West Coast. That person said: “If it takes your resigning for us to be discovered and
to get the reduction in one -way bridges, a decent hospital, and proper funding of our
education, then it’s worth it.” I thought seriously about it because I am committed to my
electorate and to rural New Zealand.
The previous Labour speaker, Mr Nash, said that this Government has no strategy for
provincial New Zealand. He is wrong. [ Interruption] No, he is wrong. It has no strategy
for New Zealand—not a clue. And what must be the ultimate insult was a press release
today by the Government’s own department, Statistics New Zealand, which is
traditionally seen as a very fair and objective organisati on. It is nothing more than spin.
Do you know what the press release says? “Current account deficit reflects growing
economy.” It then goes on to say: “The larger deficit”—because indeed it was a larger
deficit—“in the latest quarter is due to overseas com panies earning more from their
investments in New Zealand.” Then it goes on to say: “Companies tend to earn higher
profits when the economy is growing. If nothing else changes, an increase in profits
2368 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
earned by foreign -owned companies in New Zealand will in crease our current account
deficit.”
That says that John Key and his merry men have got what they want. They
campaigned on selling down our assets and on facilitating the sale of anything that
moves and anything that does not —land, houses, companies; you name it. They have
got that, and what that has left us in is a structural malaise —that is, Statistics New
Zealand, in spite of its spin, is admitting that the better our economy gets, the worse our
deficit becomes. We need change, and they have indicated h ere that without change we
will continue to go down the gurgler. Well, change is on its way at the next election —
starting with the by-election—and I am very pleased. Nikki Kaye said that we have got
the best in New Zealand. Well, I would have to say that i s a pretty poor target. We can
do better, and the Labour Party in Government will ensure that we work for a better
New Zealand for everyone.
In the primary sector, the Ministry for Primary Industries —the new superministry—
has an export double goal: to double the number of exports from this country by 2025. It
is failing, because we are some way down the track from when it said that and we have
not made much progress. It has been said that a goal is not a strategy, but the
Government has not learnt that. Although I applaud the efforts to increase our exports, it
is coming at the expense of a long -term vision for our country. I say to you that
National, in spite of its traditional support from the rural sector, is now destroying the
very people who put it in power. There is a clear lack of leadership, not only at
departmental level in the Ministry for Primary Industries, where the Government
formed the superministry, but also from the Ministers themselves. I challenge John Key
and Minister Guy to provide the le adership that the rural and primary sectors are
seeking at this moment.
Yesterday an independent group—the Meat Industry Excellence group —put
together, after pleading for funding, a very good report identifying about half a billion
dollars in savings each year that can be achieved in the meat sector, which will give
more security to meatworkers, more security to rural communities, and a brighter future
for farmers, and it will ensure that we have growing stock numbers. It depends upon the
Government taking leadership and taking the steps as laid down in that report.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Will they do it?
Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR: Will they do it? Well, I have offered personally to
Minister Guy support from myself and from the Labour Party  to implement those
recommendations if he so chooses. I am not going to hold my breath on that. The
Government has already committed $350 million of taxpayers’ money—$350 million of
farmers’ money—to a Primary Growth Partnership scheme about which the Office of
the Auditor -General says: “Having reviewed six programmes, there is no identifiable
economic benefit so far.” It is an absolute rort and a slush fund for a bunch of Tories
who go around the country singing the praises of the Government, knowi ng full well
that their sectors are slipping backwards.
The dairy industry is facing some big challenges, as is the meat industry —and all of
them—because this Government refuses to show the leadership necessary to develop a
strategy for New Zealand, a New Zealand that we want to be proud of.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Getting to speak last, or near to last, in
the general debate just re -emphasises the tragic nature of some in this House. I want to
remind the last speaker, Damien O’Connor, that he, of course, tried leaving the House
for a while and no one wanted him back, so they did not put any new bridges on the
West Coast. That did not work for him. I also want to remind the co -leader of the Green
Party that Kelvin Grove, of course, is very close to my electorate. I could throw a stone
at it. There is in fact no school in Kelvin Grove and she was quoting the “Kelvin Grove
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2369
School” numbers to the Prime Minister just this afternoon. T here is no such school in
New Zealand, unfortunately. I think that is a bit tragic too. I think that when we get up
to speak in this House we need to be pretty clear of our facts.
Before I get on to the real topic of my speech, I want to touch on a topic that the
previous speaker spoke about, and that is the Meat Industry Excellence report, which
was presented last night. It was presented to quite a group of people from around New
Zealand. It was, of course, instigated by John McCarthy, who comes a fair wa y out of
the middle of my electorate, from Ōhākune. He was very pleased to bring that report to
the country last night. It did point out some very good points. It made some very good
points, as the previous speaker said, and I am sure that if those points made in the
course of that report, and all the work that was done on that report, in fact, have the
value that the previous speaker said, then they will be brought to fruition in due course,
probably by the industry, or maybe by a Government.
I want to ge t back to talk about how improvements to the economy are making life
significantly better for our families in New Zealand. I want to start firstly with interest
rates. We are seeing interest rates —and I guess it is a great surprise to some —in a
position now that is making a significant difference to young families throughout New
Zealand. It is making a difference to business. It is certainly making a difference to the
farming community in my electorate. We have also seen fuel prices drop significantly in
the last few months, making a difference of probably around about $30 a week to the
average family. I know in my case that if I fill up in Levin, I can get my petrol at 20c a
litre cheaper than I can in Wellington. If I fill up in Palmerston North, I can get  it
cheaper than I can in Sanson, for example —and significantly cheaper as well. So being
lucky enough to have to drive down here every week I fill up in Levin as I go past,
going both ways. It makes a difference.
I want to also talk about ACC, which has taken $130 off the family car expenses.
That is a significant saving again for New Zealand families.
Finally in this section I want to very briefly mention the New Zealand dollar, which,
of course, has come off at about 10c against the US$1, making a significant difference
to most of our exporters. Although there might be some threat to us around what is
going on in the cross rate with Australia, we certainly are in a good position from that
perspective. So, all in all, the economy is making a significant difference to what is
going on in New Zealand and with New Zealand families, and in rural New Zealand.
Very briefly on the dairy prices, which have come off at 8 percent overnight in New
Zealand, or the milk price has —I think that when you compare this an d look at the
recent 1080 scare, it just shows the irresponsible nature of the type of activity that had
been engaged in there. I also want to quickly touch on a demonstration day held by
Operational Solutions for Primary Industries out in the Hutt some 2 weeks ago, which a
number of us were fortunate enough to attend. It looked at the benefits of 1080, which
have made a massive difference to the preservation of our forests, our nature, and to the
eradication of possums and, of course, TB, which has been vi rtually cleaned up in New
Zealand by the 1080 programme. Without the use of this tool we would be in desperate
straits from a TB perspective and certainly our native fauna and wildlife —our native
birds particularly —would also be in deep distress. I think w e all want to see a time
when 1080 is replaced by something more efficient, but until that time happens, I do not
think we have much choice but to continue with it.
I want to touch quickly on the Northland Fieldays, which I attended a couple of
weeks ago. They were pretty successful. I might make the point also, for the benefit of
the New Zealand First member who just spoke recently, that that party is so interested
in the Northland electorate it did not even stand a candidate there for four elections. So
that shows the interest it has got. I might also make a point about that member. He
2370 General Debate 18 Mar 2015
himself comes from Carterton —the Carterton District Council, of which he was the
mayor—which is about the size of Kerikeri, or not much bigger, and, of course, the
number of votes he got in the last election was smaller than the number of votes he got
in Carterton.
Finally, I want to very briefly mention the Central Districts Fieldays, held at
Manfeild this last week, which was extremely successful, and had a crowd of 40,000
through there. Again, there were families, farmers, and other people of New Zealand
enjoying themselves. Thank you.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Before I start my general debate speech I
would just like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the people of Vanuatu. I have
not had that chance yet. I acknowledge my friends in Parliament  over there who are
doing their absolute best for their people under dreadful circumstances. I acknowledge
them for facing the front line of climate change, the front line of no resources, and the
destruction that has come from a mismanaged planet.
I would also just like to correct the previous speaker, Ian McKelvie, on his
unfortunate tirade on Metiria’s question. In fact, the name of the school is—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just ask the
member—I know it is a habit that people have developed, with the familiarity with the
name of the co-leader of the Green Party, but I think that even if one addresses someone
in a particular way outside the House, the formality should stay in the House.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Assistant Speaker. I do
hope I have not offended Metiria Turei. Somehow I feel I may not have, but I do take
your point. We should maintain the rules of the House.
I would just like to refer to the National Party member who said that Metiria Turei
was wrong about “Kelvin Grove School”. I think he misheard the name of the school. I
have rechecked the question. It is Kelvin Road School, and it is a school that both
Metiria and I are familiar with. I have visited it. It is in Papatoetoe, not in his electorate.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How can this be a point of order?

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: For the deputy leader of the Labour Party, I say that the member has
just offended in exactly the same way that she was asked not to by the Assistant
Speaker a moment ago. I completely agree with the Assistant Speaker and would ask—

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: What? I called her “Turei.”

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: No, on that occasion again, the member’s first name only was used.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: I am sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Catherine Delahunty,
are you replying to the point of order?

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Yes. I am not actually replying to the point of order
as such. I cannot remember whether I said “Metiria” or “Metiria Turei”. I am afraid that
I am attempting to stick to the rules of the House and perhaps to talk about important
subjects, if that member would allow me to continue.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: OK, and I apologise if I
missed it, because I did too.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: So if we could get on with the business of the day,
water is the subject of the general debate for me, because no matter how many bridges
you build in Northland, it is what goes underneath the bridge that really matters. I
recently visited the Tai Tokerau in the middle north, and I stood on the bridges with a
wonderful man called Millan Ruka, who runs the environmental river patrol. I stood on
those bridges and I saw slimy, dirty, algae -ridden grey water because of the excessive
amount of effluent that was coming into those rivers from badly mana ged farms in the
area of the Hikurangi Swamp. It is that kind of problem that we saw today in question
18 Mar 2015 General Debate 2371
time when the Prime Minister was unable to answer my questions about the very
reasonable call that Federated Farmers put out that we end dairy conversion s in the
upper Waikato. When Federated Farmers tell the country that we have gone too far with
dairying and that Landcorp should stop converting their farms, we know there is a big
problem.
Chris Lewis from Federated Farmers Waikato made it very clear thi s week that a
moratorium was a really good idea, not because he is anti -dairying—he is no more anti-
dairying than the Green Party is —but because he can see that downstream the efforts
that farmers are making across the Waikato to clean up water quality are being
undermined by a Government -owned State- owned enterprise, Landcorp, which is
proposing to put another 29,500 dairy cows in the upper catchment. The catchment
cannot take it. That is in the next 5 years. It is proposing to do this, not over 30 years o r
even 40 years, but in the next 5 years because the Government, unlike Federated
Farmers, has gone crazy with milk -fed greed. And while that takes place, every
waterway downstream is at risk. The point that Chris Lewis was making is a very valid
point bec ause he was saying that the farming community has put a lot of effort into
riparian planting, into fencing, and into trying to manage nutrients in the Waikato. I
would say there is a lot more work to go, having been up along the Waihou River and
other such rivers that are still in a parlous state. But it is very disturbing to see the
Government-owned enterprise Landcorp ignoring the calls of farmers and attacking
Federated Farmers for daring to suggest that enough was enough.
So we are saying to Federated F armers that we are going to stand beside you in this
call for a halt. We think it is a very reasonable call because the people who have made
the effort, who are trying to meet a decent standard of water quality, are being
undermined by their own Government . The Government set a quality standard for fresh
water—its National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management —that is incredibly
low. It is completely low and it is pretty much useless because it is all about wading and
boating, not swimming. If you cannot swim in a river like I could swim in a river when
I was young, we have lost —I beg your pardon, Mr Assistant Speaker; not you. If we
cannot swim in rivers any more, we have lost something really precious.
We should listen to Federated Farmers. They are telling the Government : “Stop
doing this. There are much more positive ways of managing water quality.” We can
protect the land, but there is no point in the Government’s policy of retiring adjacent
waterways to land if upstream it is putting thousands more cows —thousands and
thousands—into those catchments and destroying the work of farmers downstream. The
Government should listen to the Green Party and listen to Federated Farmers. It is in
everyone’s interest to protect water. There will not be any wonderful economy, and
there will not be any fantastic community, great lifestyle, and all the rest that it spouts
on about year after year, coming from its policies if it does not protect water. Water is
life and we must protect it. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
I wonder whether you could just explain whether there has been a change of procedure
relating to the general debate, in that in the past there has never been a 1 -minute
warning bell rung, but  today I have noticed on several occasions that there has been. Is
that a permanent change or were you just being particularly benevolent towards the
speakers in the Chamber today?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: It was a deliberate thing,
which I have done during the general debate when I have been in the Chair in the past. I
think that, generally, members have felt that it is useful having a warning. Some people
have greeted it, as the member did, with some relief.
2372 General Debate 18 Mar 2015

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I was not complaining; I just wanted
to be clear so that I can advise our members.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: You will probably have
inconsistent treatment depending on who is in the Chair.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
SOCIAL SECURITY (CLOTHING ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS AND
UNSUPPORTED CHILDREN) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 25 February.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak to the second reading
of the Social Security (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported Children)
Amendment Bill. At the outset can I congratulate the MP Tracey Martin, who has
brought this issue before our Parliament. She is genuine in her concern towards children
who are unsupported and are being taken care of by family members, and she is genuine
in her concern about their equality with other children who are in similar situations. I
want to commend Tracey Martin because she has done everything she can to make sure
there is some progress on this issue.
I also want to say that I feel, as part of th e Social Services Committee, which
considered this bill, that I know how hard Tracey Martin has worked on presenting this
issue. It was with a bit of a heavy heart that I was part of the committee when it agreed
to an amendment that sees these changes not coming in until 2018. I think it is
important that people listening to this debate understand the background to that, because
that is not of the member’s choosing, and it was not the choosing of the majority of the
select committee. It was because the Government does not see this as being a priority.
The Government simply would not agree to support this bill unless this proposed
change, which brings equality to children very much in need, was pushed out not just
beyond the next election —which at the time the select committee was debating this
would have been the election we have just had, in 2014—but beyond the 2017 election.
I am going to place a bet right now, because I am a betting person, that by the time this
legislation comes into being, there will in  fact be a Labour -led Government in place.
There will be a Labour -led Government in place, and by 1 July 2018 we will be in
control of bringing budgetary measures into this House that will not only help these
children but help all the children who are suff ering in New Zealand, particularly
children who are living in poverty, which that Government absolutely fails to even
recognise, let alone address.
This bill comes behind priorities for the National Government like suddenly finding
the funding for 10 brid ges in Northland—the bridges that the Northland Regional
Council does not even want and does not say it needs. But that is a priority for this
National Government at the moment, and these unsupported children, these children
who are being brought up often by their grandparents and by other family members, do
not deserve to have equality when it comes to the financial support they will have as
they are growing up. That Government opposite would rather build bridges in
Northland. It would rather have put its energy into trying to sort out the Skycity debacle.
It would rather, actually, be focused on—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Rio Tinto.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That is right—giving money to Rio Tinto. That is a priority. That
is a priority for this Government. It will address those issues immediately, but these
children and their families, who are working hard to support them, have to wait until 1
18 Mar 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 2373
July 2018. I think that is an absolute indictment on the National Government and its
lack of priority for the things that really matter.
I just want to remind people —because this is an interrupted debate—whom we are
talking about here. We are talking about children who through a range of often really
tragic circumstances are not able to live with their natural parents. That may be because
their natural parents have died. It may be because—certainly it was in one of the
submissions the select committee heard —the father of the children had murdered their
mother, so the father was incarcerated and the mother was no longer with them. These
are terribly, terribly tragic situations in which the grandparents had absolutely been
there for their grandchildren. They had stepped i n at a time of huge grief to themselves
and started raising children who were at primary school, and teenagers, even though
they were grandparents who suddenly found themselves in that position.
So these are often tragic situations. These are often childr en whose grandparents
have determined or have worked with the rest of the family to say that they are the best
people to be caring for those children, and yet the State support they get for doing so is
less than what people who have no relationship with the children they take them on—
foster carers—get. An example of that is that a foster carer can apply for a quarterly
clothing allowance. They can apply for an allowance for Christmas and birthday
presents. They can have their health and education costs met,  depending on the child’s
care plan. The carer may also be able to provide financial assistance towards
recreational items. All of these matters should be extended to unsupported children as
well, as we call them.
I remind the House that these children who are being taken care of by family
members often have additional needs. Not only do they need another family member to
take care of them but they are often suffering a high degree of trauma, and that has
financial costs associated with it, as well.
We had several heartbreaking submissions on this bill before the select committee,
one of which I just described before, but all of them —all of them—had one theme and
that was the relatives, now the primary carers, of these children coming to tell our select
committee how much grief it caused them to see that they could not provide. They felt
they could not provide as much for these children in their times of need. So submitters
were coming to us and talking about how they felt that they needed to go to the op s hop
and buy second-hand clothes for their children, because they could not provide anything
more. These are often grandparents who are on New Zealand superannuation. They
have got fixed incomes and they could not provide anything more than that, and the one
thing they wanted was for their grandchildren to be able to hold their heads up high
amongst their peers and be able to be treated just like anyone else, and they often felt
like that was not the case. We heard many gut-wrenching submissions.
I also want to also congratulate Tracey Martin on the way in which she presented her
briefing to the select committee. As a former adult educator I was very impressed. We
did not have bits of paper to wade through like we frequently do in briefings on this
matter. We had caricatures of two children, and on each of those children —one was an
unsupported child, and the other was being taken care of by a foster family —was
written what financial support they were entitled to from the State and what they were
not entitled to. It was a very, very graphic way of bringing that information before the
select committee.
I conclude this contribution by saying that Labour endorses and supports this bill.
We wish that it had a start date right now, because these children need the s upport right
now.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: I apologise if, somewhere along the line, my voice
fades during this speech.
