items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I am pleased to rise and take a call on the first reading of the
Electronic Data Safety Bill which has been presented to the House by Labour MP Clare
Curran. The Greens are supporting this bill, which is a response to continued very
serious privacy breach es within the Ministry of Social Development and other
Government departments. We have seen breaches over the last few years in ACC,
Novopay, Work and Income, the Earthquake Commission, the Ministry for the
Environment, the Ministry of Education, and Immig ration New Zealand —the breaches
go on. We have had breaches from within Government departments and breaches from
the very leadership —the Ministers of those departments, the Ministry of Social
Development and the Ministry of Justice, two critical ministeria l positions when it
comes to considering privacy.
Really, this bill, we believe, speaks to the issue of trust and the ability of New
Zealanders to trust that this Government will solve those problems of privacy when the
leadership it has shown has run so counter to the principles of privacy. It is clear this is
a deeply serious issue that needs a serious solution. It is concerning to hear Ministers of
the Government say that there is no need for this bill because everything has been
sorted. They speak as i f this is such a thing of the distant past when the last major
breach—in fact, of 600 ACC clients’ data —occurred just this year in January. This is
not an issue of the distant past. The Green Party takes privacy seriously. One of our
members Gareth Hughes has a member’s bill on internet rights and freedoms, which
will ensure the right to privacy online, a right that currently is not legally protected
within New Zealand law.
I would like to speak this evening briefly a little more on this special need for a
commission of inquiry into the Ministry of Social Development privacy breaches, and,
most important, the need for an independent inquiry with official status to look at
systemic issues within the Ministry of Social Development, because at the end of last
year the Office of the Auditor -General released a report on complaints within the
Ministry of Social Development. Within this report it found that there was significant
room for improvement in the processing and recording of complaints, and it expressed
concern about the lack of ministry -wide analysis of complaints to identify systemic
problems, which goes to the very heart of this bill, because if we cannot trust the
ministry to identify complaints in relation to privacy and put systemic responses in
place, then we need an independent inquiry. This is clearly telling us that we cannot
have that trust because those systems are not in place.
We have been hearing this concern from advocates and lawyers for quite a while on a
much wider level. Again, it speaks to our ability to trust. Recently, Frances Joychild QC
also raised the issue of the lack of power and legal support for beneficiaries
experiencing problems in the system. She has written a very, very powerful article on
this and the need for us to actuall y start turning round what has become a drastic
imbalance of power. Again, it speaks to our ability to trust and the need and importance
for this bill. We have seen examples of legal rulings happening in courts against the
Ministry of Social Development wh ere it has not even, after a ruling against it, put
systems in place to ensure a policy change. We cannot have any trust in this ministry at
the moment when it refuses to put the systems in place to turn it round even with court
rulings against it. We need  privacy reporting to be public. We need an inquiry. Just
recently, we have heard of cases—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Electronic data is what we are debating.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It is absolutely about electronic data in relation to the Ministry of
Social Development and privacy, which is what this bill is about. We have had
18 Mar 2015 Electronic Data Safety Bill 2397
somebody contact us where they have been to the Privacy Commissioner, they had had
a ruling in their favour, but that was a confidential ruling and they have evidence that no
systems change or policy change has been put in place as a result of that ruling. We
have no systemic ability to respond to breaches at the moment. Because of that lack of
ability to trust in the system, we need this independent inquiry. The Greens fully
support this bill because it answers the public’s lack of trust.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: I am rising to speak on the
Electronic Data Safety Bill. Can I first say that I think  electronic data protection is
important, it is vital, and it is paramount in the 21 st century. Although I am not on the
Commerce Committee, I am on the Social Services Committee, so patient data and
records and their stories, and the protection of that da ta, is paramount as well. It is an
area that I am extremely interested in. I was very interested to read about the key driver
to this bill in the general policy statement, the hacking of 7,000 documents from the
Ministry of Social Development computer netw ork through Work and Income self -
service kiosks. This included medical records, personal data, and pay rates.
I think electronic data protection is important because we are using information
technology a lot more these days. Some of us are buying our groc eries online, some of
us are reading books online, and I have heard of some people finding love online. I am
very much proud of our Government, which is committing to essential infrastructure
and information technology around our ultra -fast broadband and our Rural Broadband
Initiative. This essential infrastructure is valued by all constituents in my electorate of
Waimakariri, a rural electorate. You very much need essential infrastructure for a strong
economy and for the well-being of our people.
Data man agement and protection are vital. I think back to the stories I read post -
earthquake when there were a lot of health care systems and IT systems that had crashed
so patients were presenting to health care services they had not been to before and
health care professionals were making treatment decisions that were not based on the
data they would normally have if their health IT system had been up and running. So it
is great to hear about the innovation now of sharing vital primary, secondary, and allied
health information, but that will come at a risk when you share information across
boundaries, across sectors, and across organisations.
I do not believe that a commission of inquiry, with an expense of about $4 million to
$10 million, is the way forward. I a lso think a commission of inquiry should be for an
unusual situation; it should not be used for business as usual. We do have precedent and
we do have benchmarking from other reviews into privacy breaches and information
management security. These are the Ministry of Social Development contracting
Deloitte and ACC contracting KPMG.
What we do know is that across the government IT work is under way to address
electronic data protection issues. We have a cyber -security plan for Government
information, and as sets and agencies are already systematically working towards
addressing some of these issues. I know from my own career working in health—
specifically, mental health—and setting out new health care services that you do need to
think along the whole system and along the whole continuum around data protection not
only in terms of simple things like passwords for tablets, phones, and PCs but right up
to risk management strategies and looking at issues around risk assessments in plans.
We know from our own expe rience in this precinct of using our swipe cards, and levels
of accessibility are paramount to that data as well. We know in health and social
services that as there are bigger multi -agencies working now, we need to understand
how much our patients are consenting to their data being shared and ensuring their data
is protected as it goes across sectors and organisations.
2398 Electronic Data Safety Bill 18 Mar 2015
To conclude, we have a Government Chief Information Officer who is working to
address data security and has been asked by the head of Stat e services to look into data
security. We have a Privacy Commissioner. This is why I do not support this bill. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Clare Curran—5 minutes in reply.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Can I lament the lackadaisical, ill -
informed, shallow response from the Government members on this bill. I could have
used stronger words, but can I lament and say and predict that they will  rue the day they
made them, given the very strong likelihood of further significant data breaches and
mismanagement of IT projects going forward and how important this is. Really, this bill
was quite simple. It created a mechanism that would have been an arm’s -length
approach to a really important and significant issue. It really would not have cost very
much to provide more confidence, surety, and trust across New Zealand, across our
public sector, and across Parliament around IT issues, which I would hav e thought was
an important matter in 2015 in the current environment. I mean, the New Zealand
Parliament cannot even get its own IT right and has no resilience in its system. This is
largely as a result of a systemic underfunded approach. If you look at that as a
microcosm of what is happening across the public sector generally, you would think
that we would be treating this with a bit more seriousness.
I want in my closing remarks not to focus on the puerile responses from across the
House, but actually t o just point to some real life examples and some ones that are
happening right now and are of real seriousness and significance. I am pleased to see
that the Attorney-General is sitting in the House. He might be actually listening to some
of these.
Last year there was a project undertaken around the number of computers across
Government agencies —whether they are departments or agencies, including health
boards—that still had a software programme on them that had run out of date and was
no longer bein g supported. The programme was called Windows XP. I undertook that
project because it had been pointed out to me by a number of significant people in the
tech industry how important it was for the public sector to not have holes in its IT
programmes and be  unsupported. I did that, and eventually I discovered, after a lot of
effort, that there were more than 40,000 computers still on Windows XP and that the
cost was well in excess of $1 million for extended support from Microsoft, and some of
them were not actually being supported. The risk that poses to New Zealand and our
public sector—and this is just one example —is quite significant. There are exponential
risks beyond that currently operating right now in our public sector, including a number
of public-facing computer systems that people go and use every day that have great big
gaping holes in them —great big gaping holes. This will come to light. I have warned
the Government. I have asked questions of the Minister of Internal Affairs today about
it—deny, deny, deny. He said there was no issue.
A special commission of inquiry into this would have created a responsible arm’s
length approach. It has the support of most of Parliament; it should have the support of
the whole of Parliament. It is not a big deal —$4 million versus $45 million to fix
Novopay and $130 million of extra spending on the Inland Revenue Department
system. This is shameful, it is wrong, and it is irresponsible. It is just frankly
irresponsible for the Government not to take this approach when we cannot even get our
own IT right in our offices in our own Parliament. There is no resilience. There is no
back-up system. Why can we not do it across the Government and take a proper
approach to this? Not supporting this bill is just, quite frankly, irresponsible.
18 Mar 2015 Electronic Data Safety Bill 2399
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Electronic Data Safety Bill be
now read a first time.
Ayes 59
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 11; Māori Party 2.
Noes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.
EDUCATION (FOOD IN SCHOOLS) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I move, That the Education (Food in
Schools) Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Education and
Science Committee to consider this bill.
This bill came about some time ago —a couple of years ago, actually —when I was
visiting a number of schools. The schools that I visited had children there who had
come to school without food and, certainly, were not doing as well as they could have
done. As a result of that, we drafted this bill, put it in the ballot, and it was drawn out —
unexpectedly, of course, because nobody expects their bill to necessarily be drawn out. I
took this bill and re -approached the schools to find out what was happening. I visited a
number of schools, hospitals, health practitioners, and many others. As a result of those
visits, I believe that I did  not get it right, and as a result of that I believe that this bill
needs to be substantially changed. But what I do believe is that it needs to go to the
select committee, because the lessons we can learn from this bill are ones that have a
profound impact on New Zealand.
I want to mention two of the schools that I visited that made me rethink what I
believed was the right thing to do, which was to introduce food in schools. Yendarra
School is a decile 1a school in Ōtara. In a sense it comes from the poor est area
anywhere in New Zealand. They rely on Fruit in Schools and are about to receive milk
from Fonterra, and yet their kids—all of them; all of them—bring a lunch to school. All
of them bring a lunch to the school, and, as a result of that, what we are  seeing is kids
who are healthy, bright -eyed, and willing to learn. I asked this school: “What is it?
What have you done that enables you to ensure that your kids are well fed, while the
kids down the road are not?”. What the school told me was, basically, they work with
the community. They work with families. They enable those kids to have the food and
the sandwiches and whatever they needed to bring to school —to be augmented with
some of the fruit and milk as well—and then they have the kids at lunchtime sitting
down and the teachers moving around to make sure that their families are, actually,
providing sandwiches. Sometimes they were just Marmite sandwiches, but nevertheless
they were something the kids were bringing. If they did not, the school would he lp them
out, on an emergency basis, and then go back to the parents and ask what it was that
was happening. That was Yendarra—I will come back to that in a minute.
The second school that I visited was Ōwairaka District School, a decile 2 school in
my elec torate. This is a school that relies on a programme called Garden to Table,
which some of you may have heard about. It is an organisation that helps schools grow
vegetables and fruit trees in their schools, and then helps them not only to garden and
learn how to garden but also to make sure that those same vegetables and that same fruit
goes into a kitchen. And every week they make something from the food that comes out
of their own gardens. What I saw in those schools told me that there is a better way of
2400 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
being able to look at the whole issue of providing food in schools, a different way that
will provide long-term and sustainable change.
I want to say one other thing about both of these schools. Both of these schools
banned fizzy drinks from the schools. All of them, without exception—and this goes for
many other schools that I visited —all of them believed that fizzy drinks are detrimental
to their kids’ health, along with everything else that the tuck shops often serve up. They
believed that nine teaspoons of sugar in a can of Coke were not going to do their kids
any good in terms of their health or their concentration. And when they took those
drinks out, those kids’ concentration improved. The interesting thing about Yendarra in
Ōtara is that the public health nurse, when she visited it, found there were fewer skin
infections. The dental health nurse found that there were fewer cavities i n the kids’
teeth. The kids were less heavy than comparable kids down the road; in a sense they
were less overweight. In effect, what was happening was not just about feeding the kids
in schools but about teaching them about good nutrition and making them and their
families healthier. This is what this bill is really about.
I recognise that in some cases, of course, we are going to have to ensure that children
do get fed; otherwise they will get left behind. But I do not want to take parents’
responsibility—which is to ensure that their kids grow up—away from them, because
that is not what we are trying to do in terms of ensuring and guaranteeing a long- term
and sustainable solution to our problems. It is simply fixing the problem today. There is
an old Chi nese proverb, which I am sure everybody has heard about: “Give a person a
fish and you will feed them for a day. Teach a person how to fish and they will be able
to be self -sufficient for their entire lifetime.” You will be feeding them for their entire
lifetime. That is really what I am talking about with this bill.
What I would like to see is what I observed, before I came into Parliament, in many
of the aid operations that I was involved in. I remember, in particular, in Somalia
feeding 30,000 children under 5 who had to be starving in order to get into our
programme. They had to be less than 80 percent weight -for-height than what they
should be. Those kids came in and when they came up to 100 percent they were
checked out. They were discharged from the programme. The idea is that feeding
children in that environment is an emergency situation, not a prolonged situation that
will guarantee that there will be dependence.
So with this bill—what do I want to do with it? It is not like a politician to accept that
they have not necessarily got it right, but I do not think I got it right with that first bill.
What I do want to do is see that this bill goes through to the select committee, because I
believe that the stories of those schools that I spoke about —Yendarra, Ōwairaka, and
many, many more —have something to give to New Zealand as a whole, by coming
before us and sharing their experiences. I do not want to impose, and I do not want to
see imposed, on schools a diktat from on high saying: “You must do this, you must
teach nutrition.”, or whatever. What I want to see is that these schools, and other
schools that would like to follow in the same direction, have the opportunity to access
the resources and the money that will enable them to run programmes like t he ones at
Yendarra and Ōwa iraka, and that they apply to, perhaps, the Ministry of Education, to
ask how you run a Garden to Table programme —how you connect with the local
community so that the local community is about sharing and ensuring that their dieta ry
habits change along with those of the children whom they are sending to the school.
Those are the sorts of things that I want to see come up.
There are so many benefits that can arise from replicating what we have seen in those
two schools and many others around the country, and applying them much more widely
across the board. Instead, we are doing the same things over and over, expecting things
to change. We have the third -highest obesity rate in the world, behind the USA and
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2401
Mexico. If we do not change the way that we do things, it will cost us billions —
billions—in taxpayer dollars. We cannot afford to have a society where obese and
overweight children grow into unhealthy adults and cost our health system so much in
our taxes. I want to see us move awa y from feeding as an emergency interaction, and I
want to know that schools can access, if they want to, a more sustainable, self -reliant,
and healthy programme, and that they can have the resources to do it.
Food in schools should be the ambulance at the  bottom of the cliff, but not the
remedy to the overall problem. I do not want to see kids being dependent, families being
dependent, on a feeding programme. What I want to see, rather than an institutionalised
programme of feeding, is an institutionalised way of looking beyond that and teaching
the long-term, lifelong skills that will enable kids not only to be able to be better fed but
to have better nutrition and better health for the rest of their lives. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: I rise to speak briefly on the Education (Food in
Schools) Amendment Bill in its first reading. First of all, I acknowledge the honourable
member David Shearer, who put forward this particular bill. Actually, I b elieve David
Shearer is a fine man. I did a search online on Wikipedia —although when I was an
academic, I did not allow my students to use Wikipedia as a source of reference. I was
looking at Wikipedia, and David Shearer, along with his wife, was named the  New
Zealander of the Year by the New Zealand Herald in 1992, and the following year he
was appointed as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in the British New Year
honours list. He also did humanitarian work in different parts of the world, including
Liberia, Rwanda, Albania, Belgrade, Israel, Lebanon, and Iraq. So he has quite
extraordinary experience, and I believe that he could have been a very good Leader of
the Opposition, but, unfortunately, he did not have the support of his caucus. Now we—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Are you going to talk about the bill? When are you going to talk
about the bill?

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Well, the reason why I say this is that I appreciate the member’s
intention of helping children from poor families.
Looking at the main provisions of the bill, basically —look at this —it inserts a new
part in the Education Act 1989 that provides for the Secretary of Education to designate
organisations as “food in school providers” and to set out the basis on which schools are
eligible for receiving assistance from food in school providers. Also, a designated food
in school provider must provide food to students in schools if the school board has
requested assistance and the school has been defined as eligible for no tice, and also if it
is a State primary school. The fund is appropriated by Parliament, and the food in
school providers must be paid a general grant. So these are some of the main provisions.
Also, the member has stated in the bill’s explanatory note that  “There is substantive
evidence from New Zealand and around the world that hunger has a significant impact
on children’s cognitive development, learning, and classroom behaviour. … If kids turn
up to school not having eaten breakfast, without shoes, or sic k because their house is
cold and damp, it is obvious they will not get the best start. Addressing this problem is
one of the most important actions we can take to lift New Zealand’s educational
achievement.”
I have to say that it is very hard to disagree.  These are good observations, but the
point is that the Government has been doing all sorts of things to help our kids. We say
it is important to help kids from poor families. It is important. I had a look at the
KickStart Breakfast programme online, and i t states that “Schools say Kickstart
Breakfast clubs are not only helping children nutritionally but is also making a positive
impact on learning behaviour. In -school research shows: literacy and numeracy levels
are improving; children are happier, have mo re energy and are able to concentrate
longer; children are no longer eating junk food at morning tea; the club provides a great
2402 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
environment for children to socialise together; the older children are taking on
responsibility and looking after the younger ones.” So I would say that it is, indeed,
important for us to make sure that our kids have food in school.
I also meant to mention my educational background, and also my family background.
I come from a family of teachers. My parents were teachers—they are now retired—and
my parents -in-law are also retired teachers. My younger brother is still working in
China as a deputy principal, and my sister-in-law is also working in the education sector
in China. So very interestingly, of course, now I have moved to Ne w Zealand and, as
chair of the Education and Science Committee, I would say that education is
fundamental to our kids and to our future. I would also mention that I experienced
poverty myself. All my family were sent to the countryside in the 1960s as part  of a
Chinese programme called “Intellectuals Need to be Educated”—or re -educated—“by
Peasants”. My parents were sent to the countryside to work as peasants, and so I
witnessed poverty in China and I also saw numerous poor kids going to school, because
in those years China was under socialism and everyone was equal, but everyone was
poor. So for my family it was similar.
We would say that it is important, and I totally agree with the member David Shearer
that it is important, but the National Government is already fulfilling the purpose of the
bill—that is, we have undertaken a number of initiatives to help our kids. I note, for
example, the KickStart Breakfast programme. Fonterra and Sanitarium partnered in
February 2009 to provide a free school breakfast of Anchor milk and Weet -Bix to all
New Zealand schools. The Government then expanded KickStart Breakfast, as part of a
programme to better support vulnerable children, with an investment of $9.5 million
over 5 years. That was in May 2013. So the investment enabled the programme to be
extended from 2 days to 5 days a week, and it was opened up to all schools, from decile
1 to 10. So, basically, we are saying that not all poor children attend decile 1 and 2
schools. Some poor children also go to higher-decile schools.
With the KickStart Breakfast programme extended to schools of every decile, it
targets more kids in need, and more than 95,000 nutritious breakfasts are now served
each week in the over 730 schools that run their own KickStart Breakfast club. Over 3.4
million breakfasts have been served, and we are now reaching more than 28,000
children. Also, we have our Children’s Action Plan, which is a plan that focuses
resources on the kids most in need. And we also have KidsCan. The Government is
increasing support for KidsCan, providing $1.5 million over 3 years in order to provide
children with basic necessities like raincoats and shoes. That is why we do not need this
legislation to launch a Government -funded programme to support the delivery of food
or meals in schools. We are already doing this in partnership with corporate and not-for-
profit groups.
Budget 2014 also supported our young families. For example, we invested almost
$500 million more in the well -being of New Zealand’s children and families. Budget
2014 also provided a comprehensive package of practical measures focused on young
families and those vulnerable children who most need our care and protection. An
example here is that Budget 2014 committed $42 million to increase the parental tax
credit from its previous maximum amount of $150 a week to $220 a week, and also
from 1 April 2015 it increases the period for which the tax credit is paid from 8 weeks
to 10 weeks following the birth of a child. Also, free doctors visits and prescriptions for
children aged under 6 will be extended to children aged under 13 from July 2015—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member but his time has
expired.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise in support of
the bill that David Shearer has put forward. I would like to acknowledge the
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2403
contribution of the member who has just spoken before me, Jian Yang, who has
demonstrated very clearly o ne of the perils of not listening to the contribution of the
member speaking before him and simply relying on the notes provided by the party
research unit, rather than actually engaging properly in the debate. Had he listened to
what David Shearer had con tributed in his first reading speech, he would have heard
him acknowledge that the solution proposed in this bill might not be the right one, but
by putting the bill before a select committee there would be an opportunity to canvass
the issues properly, to get submissions from the public, to look at what is happening
now and what is working, and to look at how things might be improved. I think that is
an absolutely commendable approach to take.
This bill, of course, had its genesis some years ago, and I recall the speech that David
Shearer made, talking about children in schools going to school hungry and not being
ready to learn. That is how this bill came about. Since then there has been a lot of debate
about the best way to tackle that problem, and I thi nk that the contribution David
Shearer made in the very beginning where he talked about the importance of some of
the healthy eating and healthy action programmes that are already happening in schools
was very, very pertinent to the debate and very importa nt. I know, for example, in my
own electorate that there are some fantastic programmes happening in local primary
schools, early childhood centres, and secondary schools as well.
Just to give one example, Fraser Crescent School in my electorate has a larg e council
reserve at its back door, the Clyma Park, which was not particularly well used. They
have now established a community garden within Clyma Park and the people working
in that garden work very closely with the primary school. The kids are involved in the
community garden. They have got an orchard planted, they do their own compost, they
harvest rainwater, and they grow vegetables. It is a fantastic learning experience for the
kids and it involves members of the wider community as well. Those are the  sorts of
programmes that I think we should be looking at as examples of what can be achieved.
I grew up in a family where we had one of the old quarter -acre sections in the Hutt
Valley, which are fast disappearing now as they are subdivided. My parents had a
vegetable garden. I learned at a young age what growing vegetables is all about and how
to do it. Many, many kids today do not get that opportunity. Many come from families
with two working parents, and I was fortunate when I was a young kid to have one of
my parents not working full-time—well, working at home—but if you look at the nature
of how we live now, like I said, those sections are disappearing. The room for vegetable
gardens is disappearing as sections are subdivided and people are living in much higher
density housing. Schools can do something about that. Schools often have the land, and
councils, in partnership with local authorities, have access to the land and can do some
pretty amazing things. I think that this is an opportunity for us to really look at some of
those issues and how we could better facilitate that happening all around the country.
What I am not willing to do is come along to Parliament and say that I am going to
turn a blind eye to the fact that kids are coming to school hungry, because they are
coming to school hungry  and we should do something about that. Do I believe that
Government intervention is the sole answer? No, of course I do not. It is a very complex
problem and it is going to require a number of things to addre ss it, but doing nothing is
not an option. This bill that has been put forward by David Shearer provides us with an
opportunity to do something. It provides us with an opportunity to talk about the various
alternatives and the various options that are available to us.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: It does not have a predetermined outcome.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: It does not have a predetermined outcome, as Meka Whaitiri has
pointed out. This is an opportunity for us to look at a whole variety of options and
potential outcomes. It is incredibly disappointing that the Government members are
2404 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
voting against the bill, because it is an opportunity to develop a robust policy and a
good policy that will gain cross -party support and community support, which people
can buy into, to address what is a very real problem in our schools —kids coming to
school with either the wrong food or with no food. Actually, some of the kids coming to
school with the wrong food are just as much of a problem. If you talk to the t eachers
who have got a classroom full of kids who have just been dosed up on fizzy drinks and
sugar, they will tell you that that is just as hard to manage as a classroom full of hungry
kids. So we have got to get real about this problem. We have an obesity problem in New
Zealand; we have got a hungry kids problem in New Zealand. We could do something
about that. This bill, if progressed to select committee, provides an opportunity for us to
have that debate and to have a constructive discussion. I have absolutely no hesitation in
saying that the Labour Party will be fully supporting it.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I have been listening very
carefully to the debate tonig ht, and I note that the member who has just resumed his
seat, Chris Hipkins, gave a very passionate speech about it. He acknowledged that the
Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill did not solve the issues but that it would
lead, if it went to select c ommittee, to a lot of talking about it. I may be paraphrasing
him there, but that is exactly what he sort of said.
I think everybody in this House would agree that the situation of young children
going to school without breakfast and being hungry until lunchtime or even until they
go home again is a very sorry thing to happen in this country —this land of plenty,
God’s own country. I was very interested to hear Dr Jian Yang and his speech that
referenced his own growing up and his parents’ growing up, and w hat they went
through. I would also say that in my electorate in Papakura we have breakfast clubs —
and that is generally how they are referred to —in some of our schools, particularly in
some of the lower -decile schools. I have quite a few schools in my elec torate that are
decile 1 and decile 2. We have some of the poorest people in the country in my
electorate. We also, by the way, have some of the wealthiest. So there is a huge
disparity. I would also say that not all children who go to high -decile schools are
wealthy children or from wealthy families. There are some children who come to our
decile 10 schools, our decile 8 schools —in fact, I am going to see one on Friday with
exactly this situation —who come from homes that are at the lower end of the socio-
economic spectrum, and they often suffer.
I do not believe for a moment that because a family does not have a lot of money
they cannot put two pieces of bread in the toaster, and some margarine, or butter, or
whatever, and jam, or something on the toast for their child. But we know that
sometimes both parents are working, sometimes there is only one parent who is
generally home anyway with the child —maybe it is a sole -parent family —and that
parent may be out working and not able to see the child off to school. We also know
that some people simply do not make this a priority for their children. I do not think that
they necessarily do not care about their children, but, actually, there are quite a few
people in our country who do not understand the benefit of a child having breakfast
before they go to school, because they did not have it when they were growing up, and
their parents probably did not have it when they were growing up, and they just do not
understand it.
But what we do see in my electorate are quite a few breakfast clubs for the children
who come along, and, as some of my school principals have said to me, some of the
kids coming into those breakfast clubs do not actually need to come in. There are many
children who do need to and it is great that we have got them, but in some schools they
encourage lots of kids to come because it actually takes away the stigma for the child. It
also actually builds a sense of community for the child to come to school and t hey have
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2405
got something to do straight away and it is a really fun activity; it is not sitting down
listening to someone else telling them what to do —it is actually a fun thing. The
KickStart Breakfast programme that we have got is available to any school that wants it,
and I think that is better than just trying to target particular schools. I think we had to
start off targeting particular schools because of the numbers of schools that we had to
deal with in quite a short period of time. I would also say that the KickStart Breakfast
programme is a real opportunity for some very successful companies like Sanitarium
and Fonterra, which have, by the way, benefited for many years from New Zealand and
being part of New Zealand. We support them, obviously, in all the things that we are
seen to do as New Zealanders, and these companies have an opportunity —and they
do—to help to contribute back to the very people who, by the way, have helped to make
their fortunes. That is what I think is a really great thing.
One of the problems of having yet another committee look at something is that in the
meantime these children need breakfast. You cannot wait a year and wonder why they
have not got a breakfast. It does not work like that. We have already got the KickStart
Breakfast programme. It is really feeding children right across the spectrum, and it is
also a great way for kids to start the day. I would like to see that continue, and so the
issue that Mr Shearer brought to the table is an issue that is being redressed. It is not
actually for every child, but it is being redressed, and the opportunity is there for every
school, no matter what their decile, to take this up for their children. I think that is a
challenge for every school to do so.

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: It goes without saying that we support this bill’s
referral to the select committee. Obviously, an issue very close to our heart is ensuring
that hungry kids at school get fed. I was quite relieved to see Mr Shearer say that he is
reconsidering the mechanism as it is not the best proposed mechanism, because that was
our concern too. The bill proposed to essentially provide food rather than empower a
school directly to come up with a solution that best suits their needs and the needs of the
children and the community setting they are in. So we very much share that concern
about the actual mechanism. But the intent of the bill, which is to ensure that kids at
school do not go hungry, is one that we absolutely support. We have raised earlier today
many reasons why it is so important to ensure that hungry kids are fed.
I am going to repeat some of those reasons tonight because it was rather frustrating—
when earlier today Metiria Turei’s Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in
Schools) Amendment Bill, the “Feed the Kids Bill”, was debated—to see the extent of
the denial of the extent of the problem we have in New Zealand around the sheer
numbers of students who are in poverty, experiencing real material poverty, a nd the
numbers of students who are going hungry to school or are doing without lunch at
school. If those members are not in denial, then they are blaming the parents for it by
continually banging on about parental responsibility. I feel very uncomfortable when we
go on about parental responsibility because it has overtones of Victorian England for
me. The reality is that in New Zealand poverty has doubled in the last 25 years, and the
highest levels are amongst children, with more than 200,000 living in poverty. Yes, we
know that poverty will not go away without significant changes in employment, in the
minimum wage, in housing, and in all the supports for families in need, but all of those
things take time to implement, and children are going hungry right now. We can do
something about that.
Feeding kids at school is a common low -cost option that will directly make a big
difference for these children. I just want to say here that I was very fortunate to have
spent my childhood in a small, rural school in Wa les where we ate two -course, hot
school lunches on- site. The school had three staff: two teachers and one cook, an
amazing cook who created incredible meals from scratch, often following local
2406 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
traditional recipes such as cawl, which was a local recipe that  used root vegetables and
lamb. It was a recipe I absolutely loved. I always had a second helping. So, needless to
say, no kids went hungry at the school I went to. Since we had a long walk home after
school, several miles across the countryside, it was re ally good to be able to do that and
be well-fed before we got home.
Food in schools, in my view, is an absolute no- brainer. It is affordable. It is
something we can do right now, and we know it will help the kids, especially the kids
who need it the most. Nearly every country in the OECD, apart from us, already runs an
extensive programme to feed kids at school, and some countries, like Finland and
Sweden, provide fully State -  funded meals to every school student as part of a wider
framework of child well-being. It is no coincidence that those countries regularly top the
international surveys in child health and educational achievement. They do this because
all the evidence from teachers, from nurses, and from doctors is that kids need a good
meal every day to develop into healthy, well-educated adults.
This bill is about evidence-based policy decision-making. This is not about what you
see in one school or another school. This takes a broad, comprehensive, evidence -based
policy approach, and we absolutely  need this bill to go to the select committee and
continue that conversation.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: I rise to speak in this first reading debate of the
Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill. I absolutely sympathise with the
intention of the member David Shearer in bringing this bill before the House. As a
former teacher, he has spoken about the impacts that going to school hungry can have
on the pedagogical  outcomes we would seek to have delivered in our New Zealand
schools. I do not think there is any debate over that as a matter of fact. I did listen very
carefully to some of the previous contributions, and we had one from a member of the
Opposition about what things were like when he was growing up. I thought I would
share a similar story, since we have heard this already during this debate.
I cannot claim to have had any particular hardship at a ll in my upbringing. I was
fortunate enough to grow up on a farm north of Auckland where we always had
sufficient food, partially because we grew a lot of produce—fruit and vegetables as well
as the meat and the milk that came off the land. But throughout my time at school I
really did see the full gamut of the New Zealand educational system, from a decile 10,
small, rural primary school, Otaika Primary School, through to a school that was
actually referenced earlier in question time today by Metiria Turei,  Manaia View
School, except when I was there it was known as Raumanga Intermediate, a decile 1
school and definitely one of the most challenging for the teachers and one of the poorest
schools in New Zealand, hence the decile 1 rating. Then I went to Whang arei Boys’
High School, a decile 5 State school.
I think it is absolutely something we would all agree on—that children going to
school hungry is an issue that needs to be addressed, and that is why this Government
has put in a significant effort and funding to the tune of $9.5 million to set up the
KickStart programme to provide breakfasts in schools. This programme has provided
3.4 million breakfasts, and, actually, more —100,000 or so—every week, reaching
26,000 children on a weekly basis. But if I think back to my time at Raumanga
Intermediate and think of the parents, some of whom were in pretty tough economic
conditions, I remember that they managed to send their children to school with a decent
breakfast. It may not have been anything particularly fla sh. It might have been
something along the lines of what is delivered under the KickStart programme —a
couple of Weet -Bix served up with milk, or perhaps a couple of pieces of toast and
some Marmite —but it was a nutritious breakfast so that kids had a full tummy and
could get on with the day’s learning. I think this is something this Government would
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2407
want to see happen, but we do not want to take away from the responsibility of parents
to make sure that their children are turning up to school nutritionally a ble to undertake a
day’s learning.
There are other complexities and challenges that this legislation would introduce. By
making it a responsibility of the State rather than allowing schools to access the
programme that is a partnership between Sanitarium and Fonterra alongside community
involvement in running a breakfast club, we face a huge issue with the management of
schools including capital issues in schools around setting up kitchens and spaces to
prepare food when the vast majority of parents, as we  know, are perfectly able and
capable of making sure their children take a packed lunch to school or, potentially, have
access to the school tuck shop.
Also, the funding appropriated by Parliament for education is for that purpose and I
would wonder, oper ationally, how this would fit. I do not know —perhaps the member
who has backed this bill has another opportunity to tell us more about how this fits in.
We are talking about, effectively, the provision of a social service via schools, so I
would actually be interested to hear more about that. But because of the complexities
that we have identified, plus also the lack of necessity given we already have the
KickStart Breakfast programme, I personally will not be supporting this bill any further.
Thank you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: First of all, can I just make it
very, very clear: if the Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill fails to go to select
committee it will be be cause of one person and one person alone, and that will be Mr
David Seymour. So I ask Mr David Seymour to contact the Government whip and tell
him that he is changing his vote and that he will support this bill to select committee,
and I will tell you why.  It is because if the National Party members, instead of deciding
that this is about feeding hungry children with free lunches, had listened to Mr Shearer
when he spoke at the beginning, they would know that this bill is actually about
delivering the New Z ealand curriculum. It is about delivering the science curriculum,
Mr Bell. It is about delivering the living world strand of the science curriculum through
growing vegetables. It is about delivering the material world science curriculum inside
the New Zeal and curriculum, which is the chemistry curriculum, through the cooking
and the preparation of food. It is about the interaction of children with the earth and also
the science extension of that: do vegetables grow better in hydroponics or do they grow
better in the earth? There is a huge opportunity here, Mr Bell and Dr Yang—

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: Foster-Bell.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Mr Foster -Bell, I do beg your pardon. We are both on the
Education and Science Committee. This is an opportunity for the Education and Science
Committee to look at ways to deliver the New Zealand curriculum, the science strand,
and at least two, if not three, of those strands, in a way that actually continues to benefit.
I will give you credit for the food that is being delivered inside schools now. Well
done! Thank you. This is the long -term plan. That was the short -term plan. Mr
Seymour, are you listening? This is the long -term answer to this issue: teach children
how to grow the food. They will take thos e lessons home, just as our parents took those
lessons home. Whether they live in a unit in the middle of Auckland, where they can
grow vegetables inside flowerpots, or whether they live on a quarter acre section
somewhere in Ruatōria, they will take those  lessons home. This is the long-term answer
and yet, because you are blinded by the title of the bill, you will not support it.
Mr Seymour, pick up the phone. This is an opportunity to make a difference, and I
suggest—I urge—the National Party members to actually think about what Mr Shearer
said. This is the New Zealand curriculum. This is the delivery, and this is your long -
term solution. We do not want to keep on having to bring sandwiches into schools —
2408 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
nobody does —and this is one of the solutions to it. Short -term answer: deliver
sandwiches to schools; long-term answer: teach people to be self -sufficient. Mr Shearer
said that in his contribution. Did nobody listen? Were you blinded by the notes you
were given by your researchers, which were wrong?
Look at the bill. Just because it says “food in school providers” does not mean that
they are bringing the food in in carts. It could be a person who has been contracted by
the school or is under a partial -employment contract with the school to set up those
gardens. The schools already have some part of it already there. It may very well be that
those in-school providers are the people who take those chemistry lessons, who make
sure that during the weekends all the materials are there, for the children to then co me
and participate in those gardens. It may be that they are the ones who go out to the
communities and source the fruit trees, so that we can cut down the costs. How do we
know what the cost is? How do we know what the cost is —because this is not about
sandwiches. This is about gardens and fruit trees, and Mr Shearer told you that when he
stood up at the start of it.
Listen, for goodness’ sake, to the contributions. Send the bill to select committee.
Give us an opportunity to give you some numbers around it. Give us an opportunity to
see how we can make a culture shift inside, with the New Zealand curriculum as the
basis of it, and sort out this problem long term.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise to speak on the this bill; however,
I am opposing this bill. I commend the member David Shearer. I do actually work with
him in the electorate of Mt Albert—he is the elected member and I am the list member
and we often are seen together at many d ifferent events around the electorate. But for
this particular bill I have to say that I do not agree with him that we should actually
teach kids how to grow vegetables. Well, I guess you could teach kids how to grow
vegetables and you could actually teach  kids how to cook food and learn how to make
gravy. We used to have that in our curriculum. I think that when I was in high school in
Malaysia—
Simon O’Connor: Just a few years ago.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: —yes, a couple of years ago, we did actually have cookery lessons
and we also had typing lessons, as well, on a typewriter. That was a long time ago. We
do actually have a New Zealand curriculum and, for me, I wonder why the parents
cannot actually teach the kids about gardening at hom e. Why does it have to be
introduced at school? The member who just sat down, Tracey Martin, talked about this
bill being inaptly named “Food in Schools”. Well, it does actually say “Education (Food
in Schools) Amendment Bill”.
Earlier, my learned colleague Paul Foster-Bell talked about his school life experience
and I just wanted to go back to my childhood and talk about how different it was for me
to grow up in a country like Korea in the late 1970s. Often people ask: “What was it like
for you? How many kids were in your classroom?”, and all that sort of stuff. I often say
that I grew up in a very normal Korean primary school. I remember only primary
school, because I was there only for primary school, and there were 65 kids in my
classroom. In every year  level there were about 20 classes and there were thousands of
kids in a primary school. They were not decile schools like New Zealand. Not one
single student was ever provided lunch by the school. It was the responsibility of the
parents or the grandparents who were raising these kids to have them bring their own
lunch. It was the responsibility of the parents and the grandparents who were raising
these kids to feed them breakfast. It was the responsibility of the parents to look after
their children.
I remember during cold winter days when, after you washed your face, you walked
to school and your eyebrows actually froze over because it was that cold, and we all had
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2409
our lunchboxes in the urn that was in the middle of the classroom. This was in the
1970s. Korea was decimated in the 1950 Korean War. It was almost like the aftermath
of the Christchurch earthquake. It was about children learning good education. It is not
about learning how to grow your own food and eat it because you are hungry. Well, it
should be the responsibility of the family. Not all poor children attend decile 1 or decile
2 schools.
Earlier speakers have talked about the KickStart Breakfast programme that the
Government is already funding. Over 3.4 million breakfasts have been served and now
it reaches about 26,000 children. That to me is a little sad, you know, having grown up
in a country that was decimated by war and yet in the 1970s, only 20 years after the war,
the parents knew their responsibility. Korea did not have social welfare;  New Zealand
does. New Zealand has one of the most progressive social welfare systems and yet there
are parents who will send their children to school without breakfast, without lunches,
and shame on them. That is not all parents.
I have to say that as a parent who is raising a teenage child, it would be fantastic if
the Government actually took care of my child so that I would be richer. Would it not
be fantastic? But thank God that I am not raising a teenage daughter because she would
be a lot more expensive. But this is about responsible Government, looking after the
welfare of all New Zealanders, and good for those parents who will look after their
children by providing breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and for the welfare of their children.
It is the responsibility of the parents not the Government. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: New Zealand in 2015 is not Korea in the
1970s and neither is it New Zealand in the 1970s or the 1980s.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Neither is it Paul Foster-Bell’s intermediate back whenever.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Yes, neither is what is h appening with Manaia View School
now what was happening with Manaia View School when Paul Foster -Bell knew it. We
are now in a situation in 2015 where the one major agency that is working with schools
to provide lunch and breakfast in those schools is alre ady feeding 15,000 kids a day. It
already has 450 schools that it works with, and already has a waiting list of 7,000
children who are looking for that same service. Melissa Lee can stand up and berate
parents all she likes, and regale us with tales of Kor ea in the 1970s. Not a single
statement she made has any relevance to the life of a child who went to school today
without breakfast and without lunch, and was not in a school where there was some
assistance. That is what we are facing today. Thousands of New Zealand children go to
school without breakfast or lunch.
We sit here in this Parliament with all the resources of our entire nation available to
us to fix that problem. We have already had today a discussion on the Education
(Breakfast and Lunch Prog rammes in Schools) Amendment Bill, where the Parliament
could have chosen to support hungry kids and provide them with the solution. We have
another chance today to fix the mistake that was made this afternoon and to support
David Shearer’s Education (Food  in Schools) Amendment Bill to the select committee
so that we can have, as we have said time and time again, the conversation about New
Zealand in 2015—families in 2015, and children in 2015 who are going to school
without breakfast and lunch. They are the people whom we should be talking about, not
about Paul Foster-Bell when he was 7 and not about Melissa Lee when she was 10. We
should be talking about the kids of today who are 7 and who are 10 and who are going
to school hungry, and because they are hungry they cannot learn properly and their
whole lives are affected by what happens as a result of the decisions we make.
I am very pleased to support David Shearer’s bill. It is different from the solution
that was put forward this afternoon, which put an obligation on schools to provide
breakfast and lunch. It is different from the solution that the Green Party prepared,
2410 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
which is to have a fund that schools can access, to then spend as they choose to provide
lunch in school. These are all the ideas that our Parliament should be having a
constructive conversation about, not on the floor of the debating chamber but actually in
the select committee where we are together, with members from all parties, and talking
with our own communities about how we deal with today’s problem—the problem of
2015. That is the rational, responsible thing for this Parliament to do. We have another
chance to do that today, and we should take it up.
This bill is going to fail by only one vote —do I understand that correctly —because
Peter Dunne is supporting it. That is very good news. One vote is going to make the
difference between having a conversation about how to feed today’s hungry kids, or not,
and the National Party is choosing yet again to say no to those hungry kids. The 7,000
kids who are waiting on the KidsCan list are being told no by this Government. The
many thousands of others who are not yet able to get on the waiting list are about to be
told no, yet again, by John Key and his Government and they should be deeply ashamed
of themselves. There is no other reason for members to be here in this Parliament, with
all the privileges of this office, if not to take care of our kids. Here is an opportunity to
prove that you are worthy of this job, and to support this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: It is an absolute pleasure to speak on this bill. It is an
absolute pleasure because the National Party is already doing this through our KickStart
Breakfast programme—a $9.5 million investment over 5 years, an investment that has
seen an additional 3.4 million breakfasts provided in the schools that want them. This is
a service that is reaching over 26,000 children, and is providing the assistance that those
children need. I think every one of us acknowledges that our children will be in a better
position to learn and in a better position to absorb the teaching of their teachers if they
are well fed and starting the day on the right foot. But the reality is that we are al ready
doing it.
I would just like to take issue with a comment that one of the previous speakers made
about this being a bill to teach children how to grow their own food. That is an absolute
nonsense. The bill is very clear about what it is, and I will j ust read from the bill if I
may—if my computer would come to life. The bill says it is all about helping to provide
the supply of food to schools that need it. There is no provision—no provision at all—in
this bill to do with any form of gardening or any f orm of growing any form of fruit or
vegetables. It is not about teaching children to be farmers or orchardists or even to grow
a home garden. It is simply about supplying food, which, as I have pointed out, we
already do.
The other point I would make on t hat is that even if there were an intent, even if we
allowed that there were an intent behind this, to teach children how to grow fruit and
vegetables, the simple reality is you do not need this amendment bill for schools to
teach that. There is nothing in the amendment bill that takes away a prohibition or
reduces a barrier or actually creates a scenario where it is about teaching children how
to grow fruit and vegetables. But the simple reality is this: there is no barrier. To date,
there is no legislativ e barrier to schools doing that. If, as the previous speaker said, this
is actually about a pathway to teaching children to grow their own food, quite frankly
there is no impediment to that to date. There is no legislative impediment that this
amendment bill would address or that an amendment bill needs to address.
I return to the very clear and simple message here. This amendment bill introduced
by the member the honourable David Shearer is actually about something that this
Government is already doing. It is about providing food to children in those schools that
perceive a need for that service and want to take it up. Through our KickStart Breakfast
programme, in association with Sanitarium and Fonterra, this Government is already
delivering that to the s chools that want it. It is a highly effective service. It has been
18 Mar 2015 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 2411
proven to be delivering to the schools that need it. Quite frankly, it is also interesting
that not all schools see they have a need for this programme and not all schools take it
up, although it is available to all of them.
I will just end with a very simple message for members opposite, and that is that they
are trying to introduce legislation that this Government is already delivering on. Their
bill is completely redundant. We will continue doing what we do. I oppose this bill. I
will not be supporting it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call David Shearer —5 minutes in
reply.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: First of all, could I just thank the
parties that have agreed to support this bill —the Green Party, the New Zealand First
Party, the Māori Party, and United Future. Unfortunately, the National Party and t he
ACT Party are not supporting the bill, which I find rather extraordinary because this
bill, as I explained in my introductory comments, is about self -reliance, it is about
sustainability, and it is about teaching lifelong skills. It is not necessarily just about
growing vegetables. We have problems in New Zealand. The first problem is that kids
are coming to school hungry, and the second problem is that we have an obesity issue in
New Zealand, which is the third- worst in the world and which will cost us billions and
billions of dollars if we do not do something about it.
I started off, as I began in my earlier comments when I introduced this bill, believing
that the solution to this was to provide food for kids in schools. I looked at other schools
and a t what they were doing, and believed that this was not the best way to address
something that is not a band- aid on a problem but is about ensuring we have a
mechanism and a solution to create an opportunity for schools to be able to teach long -
term lifelong skills. I want to make sure that people on the other side understand what in
fact they are giving up, because I have been criticised with this bill. One is for changing
my opinion and my mind on it, and that is something that a politician does not genera lly
do. We normally dig ourselves into a huge hole and bury ourselves in it, and in this
particular case I said: “This is not the right way forward. I disagree and we need to be
going in a different direction, and that is why I have outlined this direction.” The second
thing I have been criticised for is asking why National and ACT are not supporting this.
This is about being independent, being self-reliant, and teaching lifelong skills. I, for the
life of me, cannot understand it. I think it is a real shame.
What I do know now is that there are schools out there right now, across New
Zealand, that are doing remarkable things for their kids. I want to come back to a school
that I mentioned in my opening, which is Yendarra School, a decile 1a school in Ōtara .
In the schools around it, kids are coming to school hungry. They have more cavities.
They have more health problems, but somehow Yendarra School is remarkable in the
sense that it does not have the same scale of problems that the schools around it have.
The reason for that is that it has brought the community into the school and with the
community is teaching good nutrition. The kids are not being fed by an outside feeding
programme; they are being fed by the parents themselves, as they should be. I am not
saying that in every case parents are able to do that, and in emergency cases I absolutely
see the necessity for feeding kids. But that should not be the solution to hungry kids in
schools. It is not the solution. It is absolutely not the solution. It is simply addressing the
symptoms of a problem and not addressing the problem itself.
That is the underlying tenet of this bill. It was about getting this idea to a select
committee where we could actually hear from those experts and the schools that are able
to achieve what other schools across New Zealand cannot, despite the fact that, as the
member beforehand said, they have every opportunity. Actually, they do not have every
opportunity, because they are not doing it. If they were doing it, we would not have a
2412 Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill 18 Mar 2015
problem. But they are not, and what we on this side of the House want to be able to do
is to provide schools across New Zealand with the ability to have their kids come to
school well fed and able to have lunches in their schools, but also to teach the basic
tenets of nutrition, which will go home with the kids and make a real difference in the
homes that they come from. Instead, we have squandered— absolutely squandered—an
opportunity to be able to do that in this House. I think that is a real shame.  I think it is a
real shame for those schools out there that are able to do what they need to do. I want to
leave by thanking those parties that have been supporting it, but I believe that those
parties that did not will have, in effect, missed an opportunity. Thank you very much.
A party vote  was called for on the question, That the Education (Food in Schools)
Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 60
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 11; Māori Party 2;
United Future 1.
Noes 60
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1.
The vote was equal.
Motion not agreed to.
